articleBody:
The great Danish philosopher and religious writer Søren Kierkegaard was born at the beginning of the 19th century and died at age 42, suddenly, on the street one day. He was educated at the University of Copenhagen, where he later completed theological seminary to prepare for the Danish Lutheran priesthood, but—being perhaps too stubborn and uncertain of himself—he never ordained and never held a pulpit, though he remained a passionate Christian throughout his life and is considered one of the great Christian theologians. Kierkegaard was certainly an extreme and unusual person: a brilliant thinker and writer whose opinions were often as obscure as they were vehement. Internally fixated, he was equally a social person; he spent long hours each day roaming the streets of Copenhagen, stopping to chat with passersby about anything and everything, a practice he called “people-bathing.”

The central event of Kierkegaard’s life was his strange, brief engagement to Regine Olsen in 1840. Kierkegaard was apparently deeply in love with this attractive young woman, but as soon as they became engaged, he realized that an ordinary life of marriage and household would be impossible for him, and he would do her a great disservice by attempting it. So he broke off the engagement. Regine was devastated, and the more Kierkegaard demurred the more she wanted him. Eventually he attempted to dissuade her by pretending to be a terrible cad who was playing philosophically and experimentally with her affections (which he actually believed), but this did not work either. Eventually he had to move to Berlin to escape the emotional entanglement and the public ridicule all this brought on him. His profound reflections about this love affair—which for him involved the questions of what love actually is or isn’t, what a person is or isn’t, and what commitment, eternity, and religious faith are—never left off and may well have been the source of his creativity and the genesis of his ideas. He wrote about the affair in his work *Repetition*, which is a sort of novel about the complex and philosophical therapeutic relationship between a psychologist and a young man in love (whose circumstances are more or less identical to those of Kierkegaard).

During the decade that followed this event, Kierkegaard published an astonishing number of nearly unclassifiable works, many under pseudonyms—spanning philosophy, psychology, aesthetics, literary criticism, devotional works, fictions. No one seems to have a handle on exactly what his point of view was, because he was against systematic thinking (his works are full of passion and range all over the place) and because of the pseudonyms. Kierkegaard never straightforwardly stated his positions, so it’s unclear to what extent the pseudonymous works represent his own point of view and to what extent they espouse ideas he wanted to satirize. This is not surprising: He wrote his doctoral thesis on the use of irony in the Socratic dialogues, so irony—getting at meaning by not saying what you mean and possibly meaning many things at once, or not meaning what you mean or meaning what you do not mean—was central to his literary impulse.

To the extent his ideas can be characterized, we could say he emphasized the complexity of subjectivity, the awesome responsibility of every individual to their eternal inner nature, and the need for each person to become free of social norms and the tyranny of the crowd so as to find the true path for themselves. I have often thought of Kierkegaard as the ultimate Protestant—one who could accept no religious authority other than his own private and not-communicable relationship to himself and to God: an inherently terrifying and lonely path.

The titles of two of his greatest books tell the story: *Sickness unto Death*, and *Fear and Trembling*. Some call Kierkegaard a Christian existentialist, forerunner to 20th-century existentialist philosophers like Martin Heidegger and Jean-Paul Sartre.

Kierkegaard also wrote a book titled *Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing*. The title summarizes the book. The theme comes from Jesus’s well-known teaching from the Sermon on the Mount, “Blessed are the pure of heart for they shall see God,” and from a lesser-known passage in James that reads, “If someone lacks wisdom let him pray... but in faith, not like a double-minded man.”

Humans are meant to go beyond the temporal, to touch the eternal, to “see God,” and the only way they can do this is by singleness of mind and heart—by willing one thing and one thing only.

Kierkegaard, in his usual fulsome manner, writes that ordinary temporal life is inherently partial and fragmented. People follow ghosts within and without, and have no firmness or integrity, and whether they are conscious of this or not, they suffer because of it. Humans are meant to go beyond the temporal, to touch the eternal, to “see God,” and the only way they can do this is by singleness of mind and heart—by willing one thing and one thing only. The only way to will one thing is to will the Good, because willing anything else will always be “double-minded.” Any priority, any wish or desire other than spiritual single-mindedness will dim one’s inner light, so that willing one thing with a pure heart is in fact the only possible way for a human to live—although most people don’t see this, and so don’t live it, and their lives are therefore sadly deficient. Even the one who desires to will one thing will have trouble, because self-deception and blindness are so pervasive and so sneaky. In *Purity of Heart*, Kierkegaard details in intricate and sophisticated arguments the many ways we justify and cover our many-mindedness, including by writing books and preaching from the pulpit about willing one thing. Though Kierkegaard’s elaborate and often tortured subjectivity (his writing often seems to me to be the flailing about of arms in many directions, or, perhaps, the wringing of hands) and his Christian faith are of course completely different from Soto Zen founder [Dogen](https://tricycle.org/author/eiheidogenzenji/)’s mood and perspective, Dogen’s concept of continuous practice does seem very close to the idea that “purity of heart is willing one thing.” What’s daunting in both cases is the power of the conviction that human life must always be religious life, and that the only possible religious life is a completely committed one, in which everything is subsumed under the category of truth, purity, or goodness—continuous practice—with nothing whatsoever left out.

“Purity of heart” is also a Buddhist idea. One of the greatest Buddhist classics of all time, a 5th-century handbook of practice according to the Theravada tradition, is called *Visuddhimagga* ( *Path of Purification* ). While in Zen, purity means fullness of view, and defilement means limited view, in [Theravada Buddhism](https://tricycle.org/buddhism-theravada/) the concepts of purity and defilement are more conventional. I quote below a talk by the contemporary Western Theravadin master Thanissaro Bhikkhu titled “Purity of Heart.”

## Purity of Heart

During my first weeks with my teacher, Ajaan Fuang, I began to realize that he had psychic powers. He never made a show of them, but I gradually sensed that he could read my mind and anticipate future events. I became intrigued: What else did he know? How did he know it? He must have detected where my thoughts were going, for one evening he gently headed me off: “You know,” he said, “the whole aim of our practice is purity of heart. Everything else is just games.”

That one phrase—purity of heart—more than intrigued me. It reverberated deep down inside. Although I was extremely disillusioned with Christianity, I still valued Kierkegaard’s dictum: Purity of heart is to will one thing. I didn’t agree with Kierkegaard as to what that “one thing” was, but I did agree that purity of heart is the most important treasure of life. And here Ajaan Fuang was offering to teach me how to develop it. That’s one of the reasons why I stayed with him until he died.

His basic definition of purity of heart was simple enough: a happiness that will never harm anyone. But a happiness like that is hard to find, for ordinary happiness requires that we eat. As the first of the Novice’s Questions says: “What is one? All beings subsist on food.” This is how the Buddha introduced the topic of causality to young people: The primary causal relationship isn’t something gentle like light reflecting off mirrors, or jewels illuminating jewels. It’s feeding. Our bodies need physical food for their well-being. Our minds need the food of pleasant sensory contacts, intentions, and consciousness itself in order to function. If you ever want proof that [interconnectedness](https://tricycle.org/buddhism-dharma/#dependent-origination) isn’t always something to celebrate, just contemplate how the beings of the world feed on one another, physically and emotionally. Interbeing is inter-eating. As Ajaan Suwat, my second teacher, once said, “If there were a god who could arrange that by my eating I could make everyone in the world full, I’d bow down to that god.” But that’s not how eating works.

Ordinarily, even well-intentioned people may not see eating as harmful. We’re so compelled to eat that we blind ourselves to its larger impact. Our first pleasure, after the terror of being born, was getting to feed. We did it with our eyes closed, and most people keep their eyes closed to the impact of their feeding throughout life.

But when you go to a quiet, secluded place and start examining your life, you begin to see what an enormous issue it is just to keep the body and mind well fed. On the one hand, you see the suffering you create for others simply in your need to feed. On the other, you see something even more dismaying: the emotions that arise within you when you don’t feel that your body and mind are getting enough to eat. You realize that as long as your source of physical or mental food is unreliable, *you’re* unreliable, too. You see why even good people can reach a point where they’re capable of murder, deceit, adultery, or theft. Being born with a body means that we’re born with a huge bundle of needs that compels and can overwhelm our minds.

Fortunately, we human beings have the potential to civilize our eating habits by learning to wean ourselves from our passion for the junk food of sights, sounds, smells, etc., and look instead for good food within. When we learn to appreciate the joy that comes from generosity, honor, compassion, and trust, we see that it’s much more fulfilling than the pleasure that comes simply from grabbing what we can for ourselves. We realize that our happiness can’t be independent of the happiness of others. We can give one another our belongings, our time, our love, our selves, and see it not as a loss but as a mutual gain.

When we learn to appreciate the joy that comes from generosity, honor, compassion, and trust, we see that it’s much more fulfilling than the pleasure that comes simply from grabbing what we can for ourselves.

Unfortunately, these qualities of the heart are conditional, for they depend on a tender web of beliefs and feelings—belief in justice and the basic goodness of human nature, feelings of trust and affection. When that web breaks, as it so easily can, the heart can turn vicious. We see this in divorce, broken families, and society at large. When the security of our food source—the basis of our mental and material well-being—gets threatened, the finer qualities of the mind can vanish. People who believe in kindness can suddenly seek revenge. Those who espouse nonviolence can suddenly call for war. And those who rule by divisiveness—by making a mockery of compassion, prudence, and our common humanity—find a willing following for their law-of-the-jungle agenda.

This is why compassion based only on belief or feeling is not enough to guarantee our behavior—and why the practice of training the mind to reach an unconditioned happiness is not a selfish thing. If you value compassion and trust, it’s an imperative, for only an unconditioned happiness can guarantee the purity of your behavior. Independent of space and time, it’s beyond alteration. No one can threaten its food source, for it has no need to feed. When you’ve had even just a glimpse of this happiness, your belief in goodness becomes unshakable. That way other people can totally trust you, and you can genuinely trust yourself. You lack for nothing.

Purity of heart is to know this one thing.

♦

*From* [The Great Road](https://www.shambhala.com/the-great-road.html?srsltid=AU7gw4VGaQ8zSFlWq536-xpNrpNxeOhEwCAF-tvOG-4L9T06T8YAhbmT) *© 2026 by Norman Fischer. Reprinted in arrangement with Shambhala Publications, Inc. Boulder, CO.*

title: ‘The Book of the Human Body’ Surveys 2,000 Years of Remarkable Anatomical Inquiry
subtitle: As long as humans have been around, we’ve been curious about existential questions like, Why are we here?
feedText: And how do things work? That goes for our own bodies, too. articleBody:
As long as humans have been around, we’ve been curious about existential questions like, Why are we here? And how do things work? That goes for our own bodies, too. But in our era of modern science and medicine, it’s difficult to imagine a time when physicians weren’t familiar with all of the bones in the skeleton, how a baby grows inside a womb, or how the cardiovascular system works. Even the profession that comes to mind when we think of a doctor didn’t really emerge until the past few centuries. During the medieval period, barber-surgeons were the primary medical practitioners (yes, the people who cut hair also conducted surgeries).

As medicine morphed into a scientific and intellectual pursuit, academies cropped up starting in the late 1700s, such as the College of Philadelphia—the first medical school in the U.S.—and the Edinburgh School of Surgery in Scotland. Ethics were, let’s say, malleable. In Edinburgh, a legal shortage of fresh cadavers used for study in the early 1800s spawned a shady underground trade in bodies, many of which were dug up from new burials in the dead of night. And then there were the famous serial murders committed by William Burke and William Hare, who cashed in by selling well over a dozen of their victims’ corpses to anatomist Robert Knox for use during his lectures. Suffice it to say, some scholars really wanted to understand our innards.

Slated for release in January, *[The Book of the Human Body](https://www.taschen.com/en/books/classics/09603/the-book-of-the-human-body/)* delves into the art and science of anatomy, disease, reproduction, and more. Published by TASCHEN, the two-volume set compiles more than 950 images from over 75 rare books and manuscripts from around the world. From ancient analyses to medieval studies to modern diagrams, the anthology surveys the breadth of eras and cultural influences that have shaped our understanding of our physical selves.

Authored by medical historian Richard Barnett, the book celebrates universality and unquenched curiosity. Despite sleeping, breathing, and walking around in our bodies every day, we are often still mystified by much of what makes them work. Throughout history, that sense of wonder has remained constant. Barnett says, “Whatever they might represent, whatever they might express, these extraordinary images have lost none of their power to shock or captivate, to teach or inspire.”

Illustrations include a silk manuscript dated to 168 B.C.E., discovered in a tomb in southern China, which features 44 figures engaged in exercises of “self-cultivation,” plus excerpts from Andreas Vesalius’s anatomical atlas, *Fabrica*, published in 1543. “In all of these examples, the illustrations stand out not only as objects of medical understanding, but as conspicuous works of art in their own right,” the publisher says.

Pre-order your copy on [Bookshop](https://bookshop.org/a/96/9783754402474).

title: Dick Raaijmakers and Horst Rickels ~ FORT KLANK
subtitle: In the hands of Dick Raaijmakers, Horst Rickels and Walter Maioli, it can be, and is.

articleBody:
Can a fort be an instrument?  In the hands of Dick Raaijmakers, Horst Rickels and Walter Maioli, it can be, and is.  Constructed in the 19th century, Fort Asperen has become the “outer shell” for a series of mechanical installations designed to bring the fort to sonic life.  These instruments channel wind, amplify vibrations and create natural percussion, making the fort a living thing:  FORT KLANK.

The 24-minute track operates as a virtual tour of the facility.  One is free to imagine the fort’s history, from protector of the realm to tourist destination.  When a gong is struck, one thinks of kingly processions; vast metallic scrapes come across as anachronistic heaters and boilers, reminders that when the fort was created, steam power was in vogue.  Various sounds skitter around the background like wild mice no one has been able to eliminate, while the louder squeaks of doors and creaks of hinges suggest the ghosts of those who may have died there.

A massive blast in the fifth minute comes across as a furnace of sound: a call to arms, perhaps, or the heart of the Industrial Revolution.  Were forts always this loud?  If so, how did anyone sleep?  Today’s unmanned forts could benefit from more such installations, which return a sense of their original mystery.  After the blast comes near-silence and a snipping like embroidery; perhaps there were conjugal visits.

Large metallic dragging sounds occupy the center, a reminder of how hard it is to move large machinery.  The gong returns before the density increases again.  The very presence of a fortress implies the possibility of battle, which seems to break out in the eighteenth minute: all hands on deck!  The internal mechanisms are howling, the outer walls are in in danger of being breached, and the cacophony alone is intense enough to strike fear into the hearts of siege makers and those under siege.  Watery sounds join the fray, implying boiling, heating and the use of force. Then it is quiet again: the threat has passed, history has left the fort behind, and visitors are free to travel its corridors, wondering at its walls, its foundations, and most of all its sounds, as strange as the passage of time.  (Richard Allen)

title: Laurie Spiegel’s cosmic sounds of Kepler passed one light day from Earth
subtitle: Earlier this month, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft traveled beyond 25.902 billion km from Earth, a distance light would travel in 24 hours.
feedText: # Laurie Spiegel's cosmic sounds of Kepler passed one light day from Earth - CDM Create Digital Music MusicMusic techTech ## Laurie Spiegel’s cosmic sounds of Kepler passed one light day from Earth Peter Kirn - November 26, 2026 Add comment Earlier this month, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft traveled beyond 25.902 billion km from Earth, a distance light would travel in 24 hours. Now is a great time to listen to Laurie Spiegel’s contribution to that record — a dizzying sonic model of Kepler’s Harmonice Mundi. An Earth day is essentially meaningless now that Voyager 1 is far from its home planet, but suffice to say the spacecraft is now, in our scale, really far away. It’s a reminder that this whole project was an interstellar equivalent of tossing a bottle into the ocean, with no real chance of ever passing into another star system, let alone being found. So the project, in the words of Carl Sagan at the time, “says something very hopeful about life on this planet.” It’s a reflection on Earth’s life as much as the near-void around. Voyager’s Golden Record would seem a little anachronistic to young humans now if they were to find it.
articleBody: # Laurie Spiegel's cosmic sounds of Kepler passed one light day from Earth - CDM Create Digital Music MusicMusic techTech ## Laurie Spiegel’s cosmic sounds of Kepler passed one light day from Earth Peter Kirn - November 26, 2026 Add comment Earlier this month, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft traveled beyond 25.902 billion km from Earth, a distance light would travel in 24 hours. Now is a great time to listen to Laurie Spiegel’s contribution to that record — a dizzying sonic model of Kepler’s Harmonice Mundi. An Earth day is essentially meaningless now that Voyager 1 is far from its home planet, but suffice to say the spacecraft is now, in our scale, really far away. It’s a reminder that this whole project was an interstellar equivalent of tossing a bottle into the ocean, with no real chance of ever passing into another star system, let alone being found. So the project, in the words of Carl Sagan at the time, “says something very hopeful about life on this planet.” It’s a reflection on Earth’s life as much as the near-void around. Voyager’s Golden Record would seem a little anachronistic to young humans now if they were to find it. It comes with instructions and a handy accessory pack including a needle and cartridge — we are literally talking a phonograph record here, albeit one printed on copper. Laurie Spiegel’s own composition, then, is both the least-mentioned detail of the record, and perhaps the most forward thinking. I actually wonder if it was fully appreciated by Sagan’s committee at the time; I understand just an excerpt made it on the record. And maybe the reason it doesn’t get mentioned in NASA’s music section is that a lot of 1970s ears didn’t really consider this music. And yet — give it a listen. articleBody:
The [campaign to secure land for the Uganda Buddhist Centre](https://www.lionsroar.com/uganda-buddhist-centre-seeks-to-save-wetland-build-africas-first-dedicated-retreat-center/) (UBC) has passed $1 million, putting it halfway to its $2 million goal, organizers announced this week. Another $750,000 is needed to complete the land purchase by [the December 15 deadline](https://www.lionsroar.com/uganda-buddhist-centre-campaign-secures-land-deposit-sets-new-december-deadline/).

“What we do in the next three weeks decides whether this land is protected forever,” campaign organizer Leslie Booker wrote in the announcement.

### The story so far

Lion’s Roar [first reported on the campaign](https://www.lionsroar.com/uganda-buddhist-centre-seeks-to-save-wetland-build-africas-first-dedicated-retreat-center/) in August, as UBC marked its 20th anniversary. Founded in 2005 by Bhante Buddharakkhita, UBC was the first Buddhist center in Uganda and the first in Africa established by an African monk. Its campus in Bulega-Garuga, near Entebbe, includes the Buddhist Peace School, the African Buddhist High School, and a medical center serving the surrounding community.

The campaign aims to buy 13 acres of wetland next to the campus, on the shores of Lake Nalubaale (Lake Victoria), the source of the Nile. Bhante Buddharakkhita plans to build what organizers describe as the first retreat center on the African continent dedicated solely to sharing the dhamma, and to protect the wetland permanently. If the land isn’t secured, it could be sold for a resort or a military base. Organizers warn that either would threaten food and water security for nearby schools, an orphanage, and surrounding villages.

In September, [we reported](https://www.lionsroar.com/uganda-buddhist-centre-campaign-secures-land-deposit-sets-new-december-deadline/) that supporters had paid the $875,000 deposit needed to hold the land, and that the seller had extended the deadline for the remaining balance to December 15.

### “ Halfway home “

The $1.75 million asking price makes up most of the campaign’s $2 million goal. The rest covers surveys and unexpected costs. With $1 million raised, the $750,000 still needed by December 15 would complete the purchase itself.

Booker credited the campaign’s community for the milestone, saying every dollar came “from people like you,” through gifts large and small and through supporters sharing the campaign with others. Organizers are asking for “gratitude gifts” over the Thanksgiving week, whether it’s a donor’s first gift or their fifth. They’re also asking supporters to share the campaign with friends.

### A new film

The campaign has also released a short film, *Find Friends: Bhante Buddharakkhita and the Uganda Buddhist Centre*. It tells the story of UBC, Bhante Buddharakkhita’s vision for the land, and why protecting it matters. The film features Bhante Buddharakkhita and Booker.

“If you’ve ever tried to explain what Bhante means to you and couldn’t find the words, this film does it for you,” Booker wrote.

### How to help

Donations can be made through the campaign’s [Chuffed page](https://chuffed.org/project/201770-expanding-bhante-buddharakkhitas-uganda-buddhist-centre). Gifts are tax-deductible in the US. Donor-advised fund grants and employer matching gifts are also accepted. Supporters can also start a fundraising team with their sangha or friends through the same page.

articleBody:
Last week, the AI company Anthropic went public in what became the largest IPO in American history. Given my sustained criticism of Anthropic’s beliefs and actions, many people have asked me for my opinion on this event.

The good news for the curious among you is that I captured my thoughts in an op-ed for *The New York Times*, which they published Thursday, the same day that Anthropic went public. It was titled “[Don’t Play Anthropic’s Game](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/opinion/anthropic-ipo-ai-regulation.html),” and it opens as follows:

“By the close of the stock market today, Anthropic will have become a central pillar of the American economy. This is deeply concerning to me, because it’s unclear how many of the retail and institutional investors handing over their money to Anthropic realize that they are, in some sense, funding a doomsday cult that also happens to build enterprise software.”

My use of “doomsday cult” isn’t facetious; it underscores a critical reality. As many have reported ([including myself](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/05/opinion/ai-silicon-valley.html)), the leaders of Anthropic have long believed that AI is destined to transform the human species, either delivering a utopia or killing us all. They see themselves, with their highly rational minds, trained on long hours during the 2000s debating these issues on blogs like *Less Wrong* and *Overcoming Bias*, as the select few who must rise up to guide humanity through this next evolution.

This may sound like hyperbole, but it’s not. [It’s exactly what they believe](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jt508VjX2H8).

Some ask, “Why is this a problem? If any company is going to advance AI, shouldn’t it be one that cares about bad outcomes?”

As I elaborate in my op-ed, the situation is not so simple. Anthropic’s belief that transformational AI is imminent has made it reckless. Anthropic now releases models faster than they can build safeguards because they believe the fate of the human race depends on getting to superintelligent AI first. (Case in point: earlier this year, they announced they were relaxing rules that required them to slow down development if models became hard to control. Their reason? If they applied such rules “unilaterally,” other – presumably less righteous – parties might get ahead of them in the race.)

Indeed, Anthropic stated a key rationale for their IPO is to raise the money needed to accelerate investments in so-called “recursive self-improvement,” where AI systems upgrade themselves. This is, of course, a terrible idea, as it creates models that are even less safe and harder to understand. Anthropic acknowledged these risks in its S-1 filing, but sees no alternative if they’re to continue as humanity’s shepherd through this revolution.

It’s unclear to what degree they even care about profits or building a durable business. As I summarize in my op-ed:

“It’s a business plan that starts with a lot of red ink and then abruptly ends with superintelligence arriving and rendering money superfluous.”

To be clear: generative AI is an incredibly important technological revolution. It brings with it great promises and real risks. But the right way to navigate these innovations can’t possibly be to let a small number of people in Silicon Valley, who have been worshipping AI as a millenarian agent since well before LLMs entered the scene, gather as much money as possible to fund their self-proclaimed role as prophets who will lead the rest of us to their idiosyncratic vision of a better future.

#### In Other News

For more on the question of whether Amodei and company are right in their beliefs that we’re on a trajectory toward superintelligence, check out [my recent technical article](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-superintelligence-debate) for the *IEEE Spectrum*, which lays out an engineering case against the feasibility of AI superintelligence. (You should also consider signing up for the Spectrum’s always insightful [AI Alert newsletter](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-alert-signup).)

# 1909 Chinese provincial elections - Wikipedia

Jump to contentFrom Wikipedia, the free encyclopediaFirst Chinese provincial elections

Elections were held in 21 of Qing China's 22 provinces, excepting Xinjiang. Non-provinces are marked in white.

The Qing dynasty held its first set of provincial assembly elections from February to June 1909. Following a lengthy period of political turmoil which included the failure of the 1898 Hundred Days' Reform and the 1899–1901 Boxer Rebellion, the constitutionalist movement gained approval from the imperial court and Empress Dowager Cixi. Seeing local self-governance as a first step towards constitutionalism, in 1907, the Qing Government approved the creation of provincial assemblies. The following year, an indirect election system was outlined to fill these assemblies. They were held in 21 of the country's 22 provinces; Xinjiang elections were postponed due to low rates of literacy in Chinese. Suffrage and candidacy were limited to a small population of wealthy men, most of whom were members of the scholar-gentry. Public attitudes towards the elections were generally apathetic, and corruption, fraud, and vote buying were common across the country. Turnout greatly varied between provinces and regions, but was generally low.

The elected provincial assemblies were composed largely of constitutionalists, who were often divided between progressive and conservative wings. Some assemblymen were clandestine members of the revolutionary organization Tongmenghui. The assemblies agitated for a variety of economic and political reforms, which brought them into conflict with the provincial governors, who held veto power over the bodies. The assemblies participated in parliamentary elections, electing half of the members of the National Assembly. Before another set of elections could be held, the Qing dynasty collapsed in the 1911 Revolution and the Republic of China was founded. The first provincial elections under the new government were held in 1912.

### Background

Further information: Late Qing reformsConstitutionalist leader Liang Qichao, c.1905

Since the Song dynasty (960–1279), scholars were appointed to positions in the imperial Chinese bureaucracy through the imperial examination system.[1] This system was carried through to the late Qing dynasty, although it had come under increasing intellectual opposition during the late 19th century as corrupt and ineffective. As it entered the 20th century, the Qing empire was in social and political turmoil, facing a series of defeats by the Western powers. Despite the repression of the Hundred Days' Reform in 1898, the constitutionalist movement continued to advocate for the creation of a constitutional government in lieu of Qing absolutism. The writer Liang Qichao emerged as the movement's most influential leader.[2][3][4]

The de facto head of state Empress Dowager Cixi, previously opposed to the reform movement, had begun to grow sympathetic in the wake of China's humiliation in the Boxer Rebellion and the upset victory of the constitutionalist Empire of Japan in the Russo-Japanese War.[2] The administrative, bureaucratic, and judicial systems were the first major targets for reform; redundant and archaic offices were abolished, the functions of the Six Boards (powerful imperial government agencies) were transferred to a new set of civil ministries, and the three northeastern provinces were integrated into the administrative framework of the other provinces.[5] In June 1905, prominent imperial officials Yuan Shikai, Zhang Zhidong and Zhou Fu jointly submitted a call for the creation of a constitutional monarchy.[6]

The Qing government reduced the frequency of the imperial exams and began to promote a Western-style education system; when this met resistance by local gentry, the examination system was abolished in 1905. The government initially intended to replace the imperial examinations with a new form of civil service exam; however, little progress was made in its creation. Instead, the central government began to pursue elections as an alternative to examinations.[2][3][7] Although new entries into the gentry ended with the examination system, the class still held immense influence. Including their family members, slightly under two percent of the population were members of the gentry by the late 19th century. Although the majority had reached this status through the examination system, an increasing number had purchased gentry status from the central government, at a cost which had been dramatically lowered in the decades following the Taiping Rebellion.[8][9]

### Creation of provincial assemblies

Proposals for local and provincial assemblies were raised following the end of the Hundred Days' Reform. In the first few years of the 1900s, reformist and revolutionary thinkers such as Sun Yat-sen, Ho Kai, and Kang Youwei began to advocate for such assemblies, citing both Western systems of local government and the traditional governance system of fengjian.[10][a] As the central government began to embrace the constitutional movement, reformist officials began to advocate for the establishment of local self-governance as a preliminary step towards a constitutional government.[12]

Upon the recommendation of a 1906 state committee headed by Prince Zaifeng, Cixi issued an edict in support of a constitution and national legislature.[13] The next year, the Grand Council established the Constitutional Commission to begin a twelve-year constitutional reform process, inspired by the Japanese Meiji Restoration and constitution.[2][14] Under the supervision of Yuan Shikai, the Tianjin County Council held the first Western-style elections in Chinese history in August 1907.[15] Following a proposal by Yuan in July, on 19 October, the Constitutional Commission received imperial assent to organize provincial assemblies (諮議局; Zīyìjú),[b] in preparation for the establishment of the National Assembly (資政院; Zīzhèngyuàn) and proper provincial legislatures.[17][18] Following this, various provinces (including Jiangsu, Guangdong, Guangxi, and Fengtian) created unelected provincial assemblies with appointees from the local gentry.[19]

### Procedures and preparations

In July 1908, the central court produced regulations for the implementation of provincial assemblies and their elections. The "Regulations for Provincial Assembly Elections" was a 115-clause document which established the electoral processes. The provincial assembly elections were indirect elections via an electoral college; voters would vote on a slate of electors, who would in turn elect the provincial assemblymen. In addition to their provincial duties, these assemblymen would elect the members of the National Assembly in a separate election later in the year.[2][20][21]

Only men were allowed to participate in the election.[22] Both voters and elector candidates were subject to the same set of requirements, beyond a minimum age of 25 for voters and 30 for electors. Eligible men were required to have either taught at above the primary level for at least three years, graduated from a secondary school, held the imperial examination rank of gongsheng (貢生) or higher, held a post at or above the seventh rank of the civil service or the fifth rank of the military, or had wealth (either through a business or land holdings) exceeding 5,000 yuan.[c] Criminals, opium users, police officers, students, priests, and those with family members in disreputable careers were barred from voting or standing as candidates.[20][24][25] If a voter was not native to their province, they were required to have resided there for over ten years, and have wealth exceeding 10,000 yuan.[26] These regulations resulted in the overwhelming majority of the population being ineligible to vote.[27]

Following the promulgation of these regulations, preparatory offices were formed in each province; they were staffed by a mix of existing officials and the scholar-gentry.[8][9] Officials were often forced to give concessions to local gentry — in the form of leadership positions within the preparatory offices — in order to guarantee cooperation.[8] Some of the preparatory offices were tightly controlled by provincial officials, while others (such as Guangdong's) were independent and hostile to the provincial government.[28]

Electoral divisions followed provincial administrative subdivisions of prefectures, counties, and districts. Seats were allotted to these according to the quota of students enrolled at prefecture, department, and county schools. Manchu bannermen (hereditary military positions for Manchu officials) were also allocated seats. The central government initially planned twenty-three provincial assemblies, one for each province, with Jiangsu divided into a southern assembly in Suzhou and a northern assembly in Nanjing. The two Jiangsu assemblies were merged due to local pressure, while the assembly for Xinjiang was postponed due to extremely low rates of literacy in Chinese.[20][21][29][d] Elections were not held in Tibet, the Kokonur (modern Qinghai), and Mongolia, as they were not provinces, instead administered under the Lifan Bu (理藩部, a state agency which succeeded the Lifan Yuan).[31][32]

### Campaign

Cartoon of a candidate offering a meal to voters in Jiangsu, from the Shanghai Shibao[33]

The public was generally apathetic towards the elections. Only one voting station existed in each electoral district, often many miles apart. Citizens who were eligible through their wealth were often hesitant to give their property value to register, fearing that they would come under scrutiny from tax collectors. Preparatory office officials emphasized that the voter census would not be a precursor to new taxation.[34][35] In Shandong, Shanxi, and Yunnan, lecturers were sent to inform potential voters of the election and solicit their participation.[36] Information about the reforms was also transmitted through periodicals, distributed to remote regions.[26]

Registration for the elections took about six months.[27] As the infant Xuantong Emperor had ascended to the throne after voter registration had begun, many registered voters were listed with names violating the new name taboo by having names which shared characters with the emperor's name. In southern Jiangsu, those who could not be contacted to change their names in time had their names changed by the election preparatory office.[37]

Corruption, election fraud, and vote buying were frequent across the country. Some voters in Yangzhou, Jiangsu were found to have voted by proxy, while some ineligible voters were allowed to cast ballots in Anhui. Votes cast in Ansu, Zhili, were decided by village brawls. In Houguan County, Fujian, the results of two districts were voided due to suspicious polling booth supervision.[38] In contrast, the North China Herald reported a relatively well-organized election in Shanxi.[39]

### Results

In most provinces, turnout was low even among the eligible population. Out of 21,073 registered voters in Shuntian Prefecture (containing Beijing), only a little over 1,500 votes were cast. Somewhere between 40–70% of eligible voters in Jiangsu participated; in Fujian, turnout was as high as 40% in the cities, while ranging from 10–20% in the rural countryside.[36][40] Foreign eyewitnesses reported very low enthusiasm and participation within much of the country.[38]

### Assembly composition

The Zhili Provincial Assembly hall in Tianjin

Those elected to the assemblies were mostly scholar-gentry, especially those with advanced degrees. Within five assemblies with known member compositions, a slight majority of members were higher-ranking gentry, with only about 10% from non-gentry backgrounds. A small but prominent percentage of members had studied outside of China‚ mainly in Japan; the Sichuan assembly had the most Japanese-educated assembly members.[41][42] The average age of the elected candidates was 41.[43]

The vast majority of members elected were constitutionalists. Although they formed a broad opposition bloc to revolutionary groups such as the Tongmenghui, they were not a unified faction; the Shandong and Guizhou assemblies quickly fell into factional conflict between conservative and progressive wings. Many of the progressive constitutionalists were younger and had studied abroad.[44] A small fraction of the assemblymen were secretly affiliated with the Tongmenghui; although precise figures and membership are unknown, at least four members of the Sichuan assembly were Tongmenghui members, as well as Shaanxi assembly vice-chairman Guo Xiren.[41]

### Aftermath

The provincial assemblies convened on 14 October 1909.[49] Contemporary political and press responses were favorable to the new assemblies. The conservative Viceroy of Liangguang, Zhang Renjun, was initially opposed to the creation of the local assemblies, but described their membership as well-spoken and knowledgeable about the problems facing the country. A North China Herald account described the members of the Shanxi provincial assembly as peaceful and intelligent.[50]

The assemblies' powers were primarily consultative. The provincial governors[i] held veto power over the assemblies, almost immediately leading to political conflict between the two. Despite this, the assemblies persistently agitated for political reform and the creation of a national parliament. Within the first year of their operation, they passed a large volume of bills, proposals, and petitions, generally relating to economic development.[52][53][54] In 1910, the provincial assemblies elected half of the members of the National Assembly, similarly an advisory council, with the other half of the assembly appointed by the imperial court.[55]

The Wuchang Uprising and 1911 Revolution saw the collapse of the Qing Dynasty and the creation of the Republic of China.

Before another set of provincial elections could be held, the 1911 Wuchang Uprising led to an anti-Qing revolutionary movement spreading across much of China. The imperial government soon responded with the Shijiu Xintiao (十九信條), a further series of political reforms with some inspiration from the British constitutional system; this did little to curb unrest, and even many constitutionalists joined the revolutionaries. The assemblies helped organize and legitimize provincial military governments to weaken Qing control. Yuan Shikai, the leader of the Qing armies, began to collaborate with the revolutionaries. The Republic of China was declared on 1 January 1912, and the emperor was soon forced to abdicate. The new republic created its own national and provincial assemblies. New provincial assembly elections were held in 1912, similarly plagued by corruption. Chung Po-yee, a member of both the 1909 and 1912 assemblies, described both elections as producing "gentlemanly, modest, and agreeable" assemblymen.[53][56][57] The new provincial assemblies were dismantled under Yuan Shikai's regime in the mid-1910s. Further provincial elections, fraudulently controlled by the Anfu Club political clique, were held in 1918.[58]

- ↑In 1912, China's per capita gross domestic product (GDP) was 52.26 yuan. A metric ton of rice in this period cost around 102 yuan, while a ton of wheat cost 71.4.[23]
- ↑The dominant language among Xinjiang's Turkic elite was Turki, while Mongol was often used in communication with the Qing government.[30]

# 1909 Chinese provincial elections - Wikipedia

Jump to contentFrom Wikipedia, the free encyclopediaFirst Chinese provincial elections

Elections were held in 21 of Qing China's 22 provinces, excepting Xinjiang. Non-provinces are marked in white.

The Qing dynasty held its first set of provincial assembly elections from February to June 1909. Following a lengthy period of political turmoil which included the failure of the 1898 Hundred Days' Reform and the 1899–1901 Boxer Rebellion, the constitutionalist movement gained approval from the imperial court and Empress Dowager Cixi. Seeing local self-governance as a first step towards constitutionalism, in 1907, the Qing Government approved the creation of provincial assemblies. The following year, an indirect election system was outlined to fill these assemblies. They were held in 21 of the country's 22 provinces; Xinjiang elections were postponed due to low rates of literacy in Chinese. Suffrage and candidacy were limited to a small population of wealthy men, most of whom were members of the scholar-gentry. Public attitudes towards the elections were generally apathetic, and corruption, fraud, and vote buying were common across the country. Turnout greatly varied between provinces and regions, but was generally low.

The elected provincial assemblies were composed largely of constitutionalists, who were often divided between progressive and conservative wings. Some assemblymen were clandestine members of the revolutionary organization Tongmenghui. The assemblies agitated for a variety of economic and political reforms, which brought them into conflict with the provincial governors, who held veto power over the bodies. The assemblies participated in parliamentary elections, electing half of the members of the National Assembly. Before another set of elections could be held, the Qing dynasty collapsed in the 1911 Revolution and the Republic of China was founded. The first provincial elections under the new government were held in 1912.

### Background

Further information: Late Qing reformsConstitutionalist leader Liang Qichao, c.1905

Since the Song dynasty (960–1279), scholars were appointed to positions in the imperial Chinese bureaucracy through the imperial examination system.[1] This system was carried through to the late Qing dynasty, although it had come under increasing intellectual opposition during the late 19th century as corrupt and ineffective. As it entered the 20th century, the Qing empire was in social and political turmoil, facing a series of defeats by the Western powers. Despite the repression of the Hundred Days' Reform in 1898, the constitutionalist movement continued to advocate for the creation of a constitutional government in lieu of Qing absolutism. The writer Liang Qichao emerged as the movement's most influential leader.[2][3][4]

The de facto head of state Empress Dowager Cixi, previously opposed to the reform movement, had begun to grow sympathetic in the wake of China's humiliation in the Boxer Rebellion and the upset victory of the constitutionalist Empire of Japan in the Russo-Japanese War.[2] The administrative, bureaucratic, and judicial systems were the first major targets for reform; redundant and archaic offices were abolished, the functions of the Six Boards (powerful imperial government agencies) were transferred to a new set of civil ministries, and the three northeastern provinces were integrated into the administrative framework of the other provinces.[5] In June 1905, prominent imperial officials Yuan Shikai, Zhang Zhidong and Zhou Fu jointly submitted a call for the creation of a constitutional monarchy.[6]

The Qing government reduced the frequency of the imperial exams and began to promote a Western-style education system; when this met resistance by local gentry, the examination system was abolished in 1905. The government initially intended to replace the imperial examinations with a new form of civil service exam; however, little progress was made in its creation. Instead, the central government began to pursue elections as an alternative to examinations.[2][3][7] Although new entries into the gentry ended with the examination system, the class still held immense influence. Including their family members, slightly under two percent of the population were members of the gentry by the late 19th century. Although the majority had reached this status through the examination system, an increasing number had purchased gentry status from the central government, at a cost which had been dramatically lowered in the decades following the Taiping Rebellion.[8][9]

### Creation of provincial assemblies

Proposals for local and provincial assemblies were raised following the end of the Hundred Days' Reform. In the first few years of the 1900s, reformist and revolutionary thinkers such as Sun Yat-sen, Ho Kai, and Kang Youwei began to advocate for such assemblies, citing both Western systems of local government and the traditional governance system of fengjian.[10][a] As the central government began to embrace the constitutional movement, reformist officials began to advocate for the establishment of local self-governance as a preliminary step towards a constitutional government.[12]

Upon the recommendation of a 1906 state committee headed by Prince Zaifeng, Cixi issued an edict in support of a constitution and national legislature.[13] The next year, the Grand Council established the Constitutional Commission to begin a twelve-year constitutional reform process, inspired by the Japanese Meiji Restoration and constitution.[2][14] Under the supervision of Yuan Shikai, the Tianjin County Council held the first Western-style elections in Chinese history in August 1907.[15] Following a proposal by Yuan in July, on 19 October, the Constitutional Commission received imperial assent to organize provincial assemblies (諮議局; Zīyìjú),[b] in preparation for the establishment of the National Assembly (資政院; Zīzhèngyuàn) and proper provincial legislatures.[17][18] Following this, various provinces (including Jiangsu, Guangdong, Guangxi, and Fengtian) created unelected provincial assemblies with appointees from the local gentry.[19]

### Procedures and preparations

In July 1908, the central court produced regulations for the implementation of provincial assemblies and their elections. The "Regulations for Provincial Assembly Elections" was a 115-clause document which established the electoral processes. The provincial assembly elections were indirect elections via an electoral college; voters would vote on a slate of electors, who would in turn elect the provincial assemblymen. In addition to their provincial duties, these assemblymen would elect the members of the National Assembly in a separate election later in the year.[2][20][21]

Only men were allowed to participate in the election.[22] Both voters and elector candidates were subject to the same set of requirements, beyond a minimum age of 25 for voters and 30 for electors. Eligible men were required to have either taught at above the primary level for at least three years, graduated from a secondary school, held the imperial examination rank of gongsheng (貢生) or higher, held a post at or above the seventh rank of the civil service or the fifth rank of the military, or had wealth (either through a business or land holdings) exceeding 5,000 yuan.[c] Criminals, opium users, police officers, students, priests, and those with family members in disreputable careers were barred from voting or standing as candidates.[20][24][25] If a voter was not native to their province, they were required to have resided there for over ten years, and have wealth exceeding 10,000 yuan.[26] These regulations resulted in the overwhelming majority of the population being ineligible to vote.[27]

Following the promulgation of these regulations, preparatory offices were formed in each province; they were staffed by a mix of existing officials and the scholar-gentry.[8][9] Officials were often forced to give concessions to local gentry — in the form of leadership positions within the preparatory offices — in order to guarantee cooperation.[8] Some of the preparatory offices were tightly controlled by provincial officials, while others (such as Guangdong's) were independent and hostile to the provincial government.[28]

Electoral divisions followed provincial administrative subdivisions of prefectures, counties, and districts. Seats were allotted to these according to the quota of students enrolled at prefecture, department, and county schools. Manchu bannermen (hereditary military positions for Manchu officials) were also allocated seats. The central government initially planned twenty-three provincial assemblies, one for each province, with Jiangsu divided into a southern assembly in Suzhou and a northern assembly in Nanjing. The two Jiangsu assemblies were merged due to local pressure, while the assembly for Xinjiang was postponed due to extremely low rates of literacy in Chinese.[20][21][29][d] Elections were not held in Tibet, the Kokonur (modern Qinghai), and Mongolia, as they were not provinces, instead administered under the Lifan Bu (理藩部, a state agency which succeeded the Lifan Yuan).[31][32]

### Campaign

Cartoon of a candidate offering a meal to voters in Jiangsu, from the Shanghai Shibao[33]

The public was generally apathetic towards the elections. Only one voting station existed in each electoral district, often many miles apart. Citizens who were eligible through their wealth were often hesitant to give their property value to register, fearing that they would come under scrutiny from tax collectors. Preparatory office officials emphasized that the voter census would not be a precursor to new taxation.[34][35] In Shandong, Shanxi, and Yunnan, lecturers were sent to inform potential voters of the election and solicit their participation.[36] Information about the reforms was also transmitted through periodicals, distributed to remote regions.[26]

Registration for the elections took about six months.[27] As the infant Xuantong Emperor had ascended to the throne after voter registration had begun, many registered voters were listed with names violating the new name taboo by having names which shared characters with the emperor's name. In southern Jiangsu, those who could not be contacted to change their names in time had their names changed by the election preparatory office.[37]

Corruption, election fraud, and vote buying were frequent across the country. Some voters in Yangzhou, Jiangsu were found to have voted by proxy, while some ineligible voters were allowed to cast ballots in Anhui. Votes cast in Ansu, Zhili, were decided by village brawls. In Houguan County, Fujian, the results of two districts were voided due to suspicious polling booth supervision.[38] In contrast, the North China Herald reported a relatively well-organized election in Shanxi.[39]

### Results

In most provinces, turnout was low even among the eligible population. Out of 21,073 registered voters in Shuntian Prefecture (containing Beijing), only a little over 1,500 votes were cast. Somewhere between 40–70% of eligible voters in Jiangsu participated; in Fujian, turnout was as high as 40% in the cities, while ranging from 10–20% in the rural countryside.[36][40] Foreign eyewitnesses reported very low enthusiasm and participation within much of the country.[38]

### Assembly composition

The Zhili Provincial Assembly hall in Tianjin

Those elected to the assemblies were mostly scholar-gentry, especially those with advanced degrees. Within five assemblies with known member compositions, a slight majority of members were higher-ranking gentry, with only about 10% from non-gentry backgrounds. A small but prominent percentage of members had studied outside of China‚ mainly in Japan; the Sichuan assembly had the most Japanese-educated assembly members.[41][42] The average age of the elected candidates was 41.[43]

The vast majority of members elected were constitutionalists. Although they formed a broad opposition bloc to revolutionary groups such as the Tongmenghui, they were not a unified faction; the Shandong and Guizhou assemblies quickly fell into factional conflict between conservative and progressive wings. Many of the progressive constitutionalists were younger and had studied abroad.[44] A small fraction of the assemblymen were secretly affiliated with the Tongmenghui; although precise figures and membership are unknown, at least four members of the Sichuan assembly were Tongmenghui members, as well as Shaanxi assembly vice-chairman Guo Xiren.[41]

### Aftermath

The provincial assemblies convened on 14 October 1909.[49] Contemporary political and press responses were favorable to the new assemblies. The conservative Viceroy of Liangguang, Zhang Renjun, was initially opposed to the creation of the local assemblies, but described their membership as well-spoken and knowledgeable about the problems facing the country. A North China Herald account described the members of the Shanxi provincial assembly as peaceful and intelligent.[50]

The assemblies' powers were primarily consultative. The provincial governors[i] held veto power over the assemblies, almost immediately leading to political conflict between the two. Despite this, the assemblies persistently agitated for political reform and the creation of a national parliament. Within the first year of their operation, they passed a large volume of bills, proposals, and petitions, generally relating to economic development.[52][53][54] In 1910, the provincial assemblies elected half of the members of the National Assembly, similarly an advisory council, with the other half of the assembly appointed by the imperial court.[55]

The Wuchang Uprising and 1911 Revolution saw the collapse of the Qing Dynasty and the creation of the Republic of China.

Before another set of provincial elections could be held, the 1911 Wuchang Uprising led to an anti-Qing revolutionary movement spreading across much of China. The imperial government soon responded with the Shijiu Xintiao (十九信條), a further series of political reforms with some inspiration from the British constitutional system; this did little to curb unrest, and even many constitutionalists joined the revolutionaries. The assemblies helped organize and legitimize provincial military governments to weaken Qing control. Yuan Shikai, the leader of the Qing armies, began to collaborate with the revolutionaries. The Republic of China was declared on 1 January 1912, and the emperor was soon forced to abdicate. The new republic created its own national and provincial assemblies. New provincial assembly elections were held in 1912, similarly plagued by corruption. Chung Po-yee, a member of both the 1909 and 1912 assemblies, described both elections as producing "gentlemanly, modest, and agreeable" assemblymen.[53][56][57] The new provincial assemblies were dismantled under Yuan Shikai's regime in the mid-1910s. Further provincial elections, fraudulently controlled by the Anfu Club political clique, were held in 1918.[58]

# Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5

Back to Articles

## Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5

Published November 27, 2026Update on GitHub Upvote 11

David CorvoysierdacorvoJingya HuangJingyaSayak Paulsayakpaul

Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting more of them to work.

With five days left, I allowed myself a little fun. When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track. So I asked myself: what if I tried to generate videos?

I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. By the end, once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 s to generate, on half of the machine. Here is the result.

A seal dreams of warm sand. Generated entirely on Trainium3.

### Two goals

I had two goals. The first was to see how easy it is to generate videos with diffusers on Trainium3. Not the simple clips from the examples: I wanted to make short films from a script, closer to a real use case, like drafting a movie. The second was performance. I wanted to get close to what you get with CUDA, or with LTX's own API.

For CUDA, I found no real figure to compare against. The only one is LTX's claim of 6.8 s for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, with no detail on how it was measured. So I set CUDA aside and compared with LTX's online API instead, which LTX says makes a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 s. In the end, the setup matches it, and even beats it by about a second: 22 to 23 s for a 10-second clip at 2048×1024, once the models are loaded, on half of the machine. Not bad, considering how little time I had to optimize the pipelines.

### How it works

The input is a film: a JSON list of shots, each with a name and a prompt, much like a storyboard. LTX-2.5 does better with long prompts, so each prompt is a paragraph on the style, the subject, the motion, the camera, the light and the sound. Here is the seal film's file, with the prompts shortened:

[{"name":"dream","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, shallow depth of field. A plump seal ... is fast asleep on warm golden sand under palm trees ...","seed":3},{"name":"nap","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... a plump grey seal is fast asleep on a small ice floe ...","seed":1,"to":{"shot":"iceberg","frames":9}},{"name":"iceberg","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... the whole iceberg slowly rolls over ... and washes over the seal. ..."},{"name":"shake","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... It slowly shakes its head and body ... and flops down on its belly on the floe, ...","from":{"shot":"iceberg","frames":25}}]

Each shot has a name and a prompt, and can have a seed, to keep the take I picked among several. Shots are chained with two keys. This chaining is the point, since prompts alone do not keep a subject from one shot to the next:

- from: the shot starts from the last frames of an earlier shot. Starting from the earlier shot's last frame keeps a subject's look across a cut; starting from its last 25 frames (1 s) also continues the motion.
- to: the shot ends on the first frames of a later shot, so that it leads into it.
A shot can also be trimmed, or have a caption drawn over it.

Making a film from shots works like animation, which has two ways to go. Straight ahead, each shot continues the one before. Pose to pose, you make the key shot first, until you get one you like; then the shots before it end on its first frames (to), and the shots after it start from its last frames (from). When a film builds up to a payoff (the moment everything was leading to), the payoff is the key shot. I found this order by trial and error, and made the seal film pose to pose, starting from iceberg.

The payoff is iceberg: the iceberg rolls over, and its wave drenches the seal. nap, the sleeping seal, ends on the first 9 frames of iceberg (to), so that the seal, the floe and the iceberg stay the same into the payoff. shake starts from the last 25 frames of iceberg (from): the dripping seal shakes off the water and flops down on the floe. The dream is made on its own, and a cut joins it to the rest.

The seal film's shot chain. iceberg, the payoff, is made first; nap ends on its first 9 frames and shake starts from its last 25, so the seal, the floe and the iceberg stay the same.

On the diffusers side, three pipelines share the models of LTX-2.5. LTX2Pipeline makes the shots from their prompt alone, and LTX2ConditionPipeline makes the shots that start or end on frames of another shot. These two follow the two-stage distilled recipe of the model card: 8 steps, then the third pipeline, LTX2LatentUpsamplePipeline, upscales the latents ×2 before 3 final steps.

The diffusers pipelines do all of the generation. The film part is about 160 lines of Python on top: read the film file, order the shots so each keyframe exists before the shot that needs it, and cut the frames to hand over; then trim, caption, even out the sound and assemble the film. The code is in dacorvo/video-generation. The films I kept are in the dacorvo/video-generation bucket, with their JSON files: the seal, the fox, and the goat, which trims two of its shots and draws a caption over its payoff.

The fox film: a walk in the snow, made "straight ahead": each shot continues the one before.The goat film: two trimmed shots, and a caption drawn over the payoff.

### Running on Trainium3

Out of the box, the model does not run on the NeuronCores: the transformer does not fit on one, and diffusers has no plan to split it. The first attempt that ran (the model card's pipeline, with the transformer split over 4 cores and a few patches) took about 5 min 20 s for a 10-second clip, and the NeuronCores were actually computing for only about 45 s of it. What's more, the target resolution was out of reach.

Five days later:

10-second clip with soundNeuronCoresWall timeOn the NeuronCoresvs. first attemptFirst attempt, 960×54445 min 20 s45 s1×Optimized, 2048×1024 (~4× more pixels)3222 to 23 s15 s14×

Getting there took three kinds of work: making the model run on the NeuronCores (requires tensor parallelism), splitting it over more of them (sequence parallelism), and making the host keep up with them.

TP-4 × SP-8: 32 cores on one clip. The weights split 4 ways, one band of every layer per core; the video tokens split 8 ways, one stretch of the clip per chip.

Most of the fixes below are on the device, and that is where most of the effort went. The biggest end-to-end savings came from the host: the low-hanging fruit, since that is obviously where the waste was.

### What it took to make it work

### What it took to make it fast

# Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5

Back to Articles

## Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5

Published November 27, 2026Update on GitHub Upvote 11

David CorvoysierdacorvoJingya HuangJingyaSayak Paulsayakpaul

Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting more of them to work.

With five days left, I allowed myself a little fun. When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track. So I asked myself: what if I tried to generate videos?

I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. By the end, once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 s to generate, on half of the machine. Here is the result.

A seal dreams of warm sand. Generated entirely on Trainium3.

### Two goals

I had two goals. The first was to see how easy it is to generate videos with diffusers on Trainium3. Not the simple clips from the examples: I wanted to make short films from a script, closer to a real use case, like drafting a movie. The second was performance. I wanted to get close to what you get with CUDA, or with LTX's own API.

For CUDA, I found no real figure to compare against. The only one is LTX's claim of 6.8 s for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, with no detail on how it was measured. So I set CUDA aside and compared with LTX's online API instead, which LTX says makes a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 s. In the end, the setup matches it, and even beats it by about a second: 22 to 23 s for a 10-second clip at 2048×1024, once the models are loaded, on half of the machine. Not bad, considering how little time I had to optimize the pipelines.

### How it works

The input is a film: a JSON list of shots, each with a name and a prompt, much like a storyboard. LTX-2.5 does better with long prompts, so each prompt is a paragraph on the style, the subject, the motion, the camera, the light and the sound. Here is the seal film's file, with the prompts shortened:

[{"name":"dream","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, shallow depth of field. A plump seal ... is fast asleep on warm golden sand under palm trees ...","seed":3},{"name":"nap","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... a plump grey seal is fast asleep on a small ice floe ...","seed":1,"to":{"shot":"iceberg","frames":9}},{"name":"iceberg","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... the whole iceberg slowly rolls over ... and washes over the seal. ..."},{"name":"shake","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... It slowly shakes its head and body ... and flops down on its belly on the floe, ...","from":{"shot":"iceberg","frames":25}}]

Each shot has a name and a prompt, and can have a seed, to keep the take I picked among several. Shots are chained with two keys. This chaining is the point, since prompts alone do not keep a subject from one shot to the next:

- from: the shot starts from the last frames of an earlier shot. Starting from the earlier shot's last frame keeps a subject's look across a cut; starting from its last 25 frames (1 s) also continues the motion.
- to: the shot ends on the first frames of a later shot, so that it leads into it.
A shot can also be trimmed, or have a caption drawn over it.

Making a film from shots works like animation, which has two ways to go. Straight ahead, each shot continues the one before. Pose to pose, you make the key shot first, until you get one you like; then the shots before it end on its first frames (to), and the shots after it start from its last frames (from). When a film builds up to a payoff (the moment everything was leading to), the payoff is the key shot. I found this order by trial and error, and made the seal film pose to pose, starting from iceberg.

The payoff is iceberg: the iceberg rolls over, and its wave drenches the seal. nap, the sleeping seal, ends on the first 9 frames of iceberg (to), so that the seal, the floe and the iceberg stay the same into the payoff. shake starts from the last 25 frames of iceberg (from): the dripping seal shakes off the water and flops down on the floe. The dream is made on its own, and a cut joins it to the rest.

The seal film's shot chain. iceberg, the payoff, is made first; nap ends on its first 9 frames and shake starts from its last 25, so the seal, the floe and the iceberg stay the same.

On the diffusers side, three pipelines share the models of LTX-2.5. LTX2Pipeline makes the shots from their prompt alone, and LTX2ConditionPipeline makes the shots that start or end on frames of another shot. These two follow the two-stage distilled recipe of the model card: 8 steps, then the third pipeline, LTX2LatentUpsamplePipeline, upscales the latents ×2 before 3 final steps.

The diffusers pipelines do all of the generation. The film part is about 160 lines of Python on top: read the film file, order the shots so each keyframe exists before the shot that needs it, and cut the frames to hand over; then trim, caption, even out the sound and assemble the film. The code is in dacorvo/video-generation. The films I kept are in the dacorvo/video-generation bucket, with their JSON files: the seal, the fox, and the goat, which trims two of its shots and draws a caption over its payoff.

The fox film: a walk in the snow, made "straight ahead": each shot continues the one before.The goat film: two trimmed shots, and a caption drawn over the payoff.

### Running on Trainium3

Out of the box, the model does not run on the NeuronCores: the transformer does not fit on one, and diffusers has no plan to split it. The first attempt that ran (the model card's pipeline, with the transformer split over 4 cores and a few patches) took about 5 min 20 s for a 10-second clip, and the NeuronCores were actually computing for only about 45 s of it. What's more, the target resolution was out of reach.

Five days later:

10-second clip with soundNeuronCoresWall timeOn the NeuronCoresvs. first attemptFirst attempt, 960×54445 min 20 s45 s1×Optimized, 2048×1024 (~4× more pixels)3222 to 23 s15 s14×

Getting there took three kinds of work: making the model run on the NeuronCores (requires tensor parallelism), splitting it over more of them (sequence parallelism), and making the host keep up with them.

TP-4 × SP-8: 32 cores on one clip. The weights split 4 ways, one band of every layer per core; the video tokens split 8 ways, one stretch of the clip per chip.

Most of the fixes below are on the device, and that is where most of the effort went. The biggest end-to-end savings came from the host: the low-hanging fruit, since that is obviously where the waste was.

articleBody:
[Quill Kukla](https://www.quillrkukla.xyz/), who recently resigned from their position at as professor of philosophy at [Georgetown University](https://philosophy.georgetown.edu/), has accepted a position as Chair of Social Philosophy of Science and Language at [Leibniz University Hannover](https://www.philos.uni-hannover.de/en/) (LUH).

Professor Kukla works across a wide range of areas, including philosophy of place, philosophy of geography, ethics, applied philosophy of science, philosophy of language, epistemology, disability studies,, philosophy of health and medicine, and aesthetics. Their recent books include *Sex Beyond ‘Yes!’: Pleasure and Agency for Everyone* (2025) and *City Living: How Urban Spaces and Urban Dwellers Make One Another* (2021). You can learn more about their work [↗ quillrkukla.xyz](https://www.quillrkukla.xyz/research).

At LUH, Kukla will be working on their ERC-funded project, *TERRAINS: Territory, Agency, and Inhabiting Space*, the details of which (including open positions) can be found [↗ quillrkukla.xyz](https://www.quillrkukla.xyz/terrains).

In addition to their new position as Chair in Social Philosophy of Science and Language, at LUH Kukla is also a Humboldt Visiting Researcher as well as an affiliate of the [SOCRATES Centre for Advanced Studies](https://www.socrates.uni-hannover.de/en/).

articleBody:
Built in 1840, this one-room School House served as the educational center for all of the first to eighth grade children in the Hockanum area, later serving only up to sixth grade. This was one of several school houses serving small neighborhood communities around Hadley.

A 1647 Massachusetts law required all towns with 50 or more families to hire a teacher to instruct their children in reading and writing. Parents and students contributed to their school in the form of money, goods, supplies, and chores.

These were one-room schoolhouses, on land that was usually donated. Most schools had one book, the "New England Primer," that was used to teach the alphabet, syllables, and prayer.

The last class to go through this school was in 1933. By then, it was more economical to bus students to the center of town than to keep the neighborhood school houses open.

Along with the outhouse next to it, the Hockanum School House was, and still is, taken care of by the Hockanum community.
