Though it could hardly have made a dent in the popularity of TV dinners, Claiborne’s typically waspish aside did draw a letter of objection from one Rosalie Levine of L…
articleBody:
“Taste — the mouth’s response to the sensation of eating and drinking — is a strange and complex and complicated thing,” [writes New York Times food editor Craig Claiborne](https://www.nytimes.com/1976/11/22/archives/westchester-weekly-what-taste-means-to-one-man-in-the-kitchen.html?eafs_enabled=false). “I am convinced that there are a multitude of people (Americans, mostly, to judge by the people who buy TV dinners and frozen pizzas) who have no taste whatsoever.” That column was published almost exactly 50 years ago, but even at that point, such convenience-oriented food products had already enjoyed prominence in American life for two decades. Though it could hardly have made a dent in the popularity of TV dinners, Claiborne’s typically waspish aside did draw a [letter of objection](https://www.nytimes.com/1977/01/12/archives/westchester-weekly-letters.html) from one Rosalie Levine of Lakewood, California.

“I live alone, I must control my weight. I am not a skilled cook,” she writes. The TV dinner’s price “cannot possibly be bettered”; what’s more, “each oven-ready dinner takes only half an hour’s worth of gas to prepare, and there are no pots or pans to clean up afterward.” While none of these advantages were accidental, the oft-told story of the concept’s emergence begins with a corporate crisis.

“In 1953, someone at Swanson colossally miscalculated the level of the American appetite for Thanksgiving turkey, leaving the company with some 260 tons of frozen birds,” [as Smithsonian.com’s Owen Edwards tells it](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/tray-bon-96872641/). “Inspired by the trays of pre-prepared food served on airlines,” Swanson salesman Gerry Thomas set the machinery in motion to package the unwanted meat with gravy and sides like cornbread and sweet potatoes, ready for stocking in America’s frozen-food aisles.

The following year, Swanson sold ten million such “TV dinners,” a name attributed to both the shape of the boxes and the form of entertainment families tended to enjoy while eating the meals within. “In 1950, only 9 percent of U.S. households had television sets — but by 1955, the number had risen to more than 64 percent, and by 1960, to more than 87 percent,” writes Kovie Biakolo in [a more recent Smithsonian piece](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/brief-history-tv-dinner-180976039/). (Among the Smithsonian Institution’s holdings, incidentally, is [an original Swanson TV dinner tray](https://www.si.edu/object/swanson-tv-dinner-tray%3Anmah_741033).) Another breakthrough came with the introduction of microwave-safe trays, bringing total preparation time under ten minutes. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Americans rekindled their love affair with frozen meals, “spending nearly 50 percent more on them in April 2020 over April 2019.”

Where holiday and commercial lore intersect, the details tend to get complicated. Swanson’s TV dinner did have its precedents: the core technology for quick-freezing packaged foods was invented over a century ago by entrepreneur Clarence Birdseye (he of the Birds Eye peas Edwards remembers as “little cryogenic miracles”), and in the late 1940s, different companies planned or attempted to bring frozen meals to market under brands like Strato-Plates, FridgiDinners, and One-Eyed Eskimo. None of those names tapped into the technology transforming not just American mass culture, but also the American way of life. In the fifties, associations with television (and, indeed, with air travel) carried a kind of sophistication they certainly don’t have today. Perhaps Craig Claiborne would be pleased that Americans never quite accepted microwaved TV dinners as a substitute for the Thanksgiving meal; what he’d think of the food they order through their apps is another matter entirely.

title: Wenn Wissenschaftskommunikation zur Sicherheitsfrage wird
subtitle: Neue Technologien können Sicherheitsrisiken bergen, zugleich werden ihre Gefahren mitunter überschätzt.

articleBody:
Neue Technologien können Sicherheitsrisiken bergen, zugleich werden ihre Gefahren mitunter überschätzt. Elisabeth Waczek vom Peace Research Institute Frankfurt (PRIF) erklärt, wie Wissenschaftskommunikation zu einer differenzierten Debatte über sicherheitsrelevante Forschung beitragen kann.

**Elisabeth Waczek** ist studierte Philosophin und Referentin für Wissenstransfer am PRIF – Leibniz-Institut für Friedens- und Konfliktforschung. Einer ihrer Schwerpunkte liegt in der Wissenschaftskommunikation des [Clusters Natur- und Technikwissenschaftliche Rüstungskontrollforschung (CNTR)](https://www.prif.org/forschung/cntr), an der Schnittstelle von Technologie und Sicherheit.

**Seit dem russischen Angriff auf die Ukraine wird deutlich intensiver über Sicherheit und militärische Technologien diskutiert. Spüren Sie seit der Gründung Ihres Forschungsclusters 2023 ein wachsendes Interesse an Ihrer Arbeit?**

Wir spüren definitiv ein wachsendes Interesse.

Unser Fokus liegt auf Rüstungskontrolle im weiteren Sinne. Wir beschäftigen uns mit der Schnittstelle von Technologie und Sicherheit. Zu Beginn habe ich es als eine deutlich größere Herausforderung wahrgenommen, die Relevanz dessen zu erklären. Mittlerweile merke ich: Das haben viele Leute auf dem Schirm. Diese Themen sind stark ins Bewusstsein gerückt. Viele Leute in Europa haben nun das Gefühl, wir müssen uns wieder stärker mit dem Thema Sicherheit auseinandersetzen.

**Ihr Forschungscluster beschäftigt sich mit Technologien, die bestehende Machtverhältnisse verändern könnten. Woran erkennen Sie, dass eine technologische Entwicklung über die Fachcommunity hinaus sicherheitspolitisch relevant wird?**

Unsere Mitarbeitenden aus den Sozialwissenschaften und aus den Natur- und Technikwissenschaften kommen gemeinsam zu einer Einschätzung: Ist das eine Entwicklung, die disruptives Potenzial hat?

Konkret bedeutet das zum Beispiel: Lassen sich neue Technologien oder Forschungsergebnisse missbrauchen, um Waffen herzustellen? Welche Akteur*innen könnten Zugang bekommen, die ihn zuvor nicht hatten? Reicht bestehende Regulierung noch aus, um schädliche – vielleicht auch unbeabsichtigte – Folgen zu minimieren? Gefährlich wird es zum Beispiel, wenn Technologie die Dynamiken so stark beschleunigt, dass deeskalierende Instrumente wie die Rüstungskontrolle nicht mehr Schritt halten können, oder wenn sich nicht mehr feststellen lässt, woher eine Bedrohung kommt.

Interessanterweise kommen unsere Wissenschaftler*innen auch immer wieder zu der Einschätzung, dass dieses disruptive Potenzial gar nicht so dramatisch ist. Oft geht dem viel Hype voraus und besonders reißerische, aber vielleicht eher unwahrscheinliche Szenarien bekommen viel Aufmerksamkeit. Beim Thema KI zum Beispiel. Da ist es Aufgabe der Wissenschaft, erst einmal einen nüchterneren Blick einzunehmen und zu schauen: Wie gefährlich ist das denn wirklich? Welche Anwendungen haben das größte Potenzial negativer Auswirkungen und wo liegen womöglich auch Chancen? Am Ende kommt oft so etwas dabei raus wie: Ja, man muss das Thema ernst nehmen, aber man sollte nicht in Panik verfallen.

**Wenn Sie sich etwas für die gesellschaftliche Debatte über sicherheitsrelevante Forschung wünschen könnten: Was sollte die Öffentlichkeit aus Ihrer Sicht besser verstehen, um einen informierten Umgang mit diesen Themen zu ermöglichen?**

### Cluster Natur- und Technikwissenschaftliche Rüstungskontrollforschung (CNTR)

Das CNTR am PRIF untersucht, wie neue Technologien und wissenschaftliche Entwicklungen die internationale Sicherheit beeinflussen. Forschende aus verschiedenen Disziplinen analysieren mögliche Risiken und Chancen technologischer Innovationen und entwickeln Empfehlungen, um die internationale Rüstungskontrolle zu stärken.

Ein Beispiel: Ich war auf einer Tagung, bei der die Sprache auf das Thema Dual-Use-Forschung kam. Das sind Forschung oder Technologien, die legitime zivile Anwendungen haben, aber auch in militärischer Weise gebraucht oder in illegitimer Weise missbraucht werden können.

Auf dieser Tagung hat jemand gesagt: „Ist doch ganz klar, Dual-Use-Forschung sollten wir einfach nicht machen.“ Das ist ein häufiges Missverständnis. Mittlerweile haben so viele Forschungsbereiche einen Dual-Use-Charakter, etwa große Teile der Informatik oder Medizin. In der Kommunikation tragen wir die Verantwortung, zu sagen: Nur weil eine Forschung Sicherheitsrisiken in sich trägt, ist diese Forschung nicht automatisch schlecht oder illegitim. Sie kann trotzdem wichtig sein.

Auch bei der Diskussion um Zivilklauseln, die in den letzten Jahren ziemlich intensiv geführt wurde, ist es wichtig, sich vor Augen zu führen, welche Funktion solche Instrumente überhaupt haben. Natürlich ist die Wissenschaftsfreiheit im Grundgesetz verankert. Genauso ist im Grundgesetz verankert, dass man als Forschende*r nicht einfach Massenvernichtungswaffen entwickeln kann. Interessant sind vor allem die Graubereiche, in denen Forschende viel Eigenverantwortung tragen müssen.

Es ist wichtig, dass Forschende mit dieser Verantwortung durch institutionelle Strukturen unterstützt werden. In der Wissenschaftskommunikation tragen wir dazu bei, das Bewusstsein für diese Themen zu schärfen.

**Wie gelingt es, im Diskurs um sicherheitsrelevante Forschung berechtigte Sorgen zu adressieren, ohne zu dramatisieren oder zu verharmlosen?**

Es ist wichtig zu beobachten, mit welchen Vokabeln und Bildsprache der Diskurs stattfindet, und das immer wieder kritisch zu reflektieren. Wir versuchen generell, Darstellungen, die als kriegs- oder gewaltbejahend empfunden werden können, zu vermeiden, ebenso martialische Bildsprache.

Wenn man Kommunikation als Handwerk lernt, bekommt man bestimmte Best Practices mit: wie Menschen Informationen aufnehmen und wie man Gehör findet. Dazu gehören Mittel wie: klare Botschaften, starke Verben, einfache Sätze, die im Gedächtnis bleiben. Wir müssen uns im Wettbewerb um Aufmerksamkeit gegen eine Flut an Desinformationen durchsetzen und brauchen diese Techniken. Aber gleichzeitig entziehen sich wissenschaftliche Inhalte durch die gebotene Nuancierung oft diesen Best-Practice-Leitlinien.

Diese grundlegende Spannung, die man in der Wissenschaftskommunikation immer hat, verstärkt sich im Umfeld sicherheitsrelevanter Forschung noch einmal mehr.

### „Die Kommunikation sicherheitsrelevanter Themen hat jedoch selbst eine sicherheitsrelevante Komponente“

Elisabeth Waczek

**Ihr Forschungscluster vereint naturwissenschaftliche und sozialwissenschaftliche Perspektiven. Wie wirkt sich dieser interdisziplinäre Ansatz auf die Art und Weise, wie Sie Forschungsergebnisse kommunizieren, aus?**

Eine spannende Alltagsbeobachtung für die Wissenschaftskommunikation ist, dass Menschen verschiedene Disziplinen unterschiedlich wahrnehmen. Bei manchen Disziplinen erkennen sie die erforderliche Fachexpertise leichter, bei anderen haben sie das Gefühl, jede*r könne mitreden.

Die Philosophie fällt dem manchmal stärker zum Opfer, weil sie viele Begriffe und Konzepte verwendet, die jeder im Alltag verwendet und kennt. Deswegen gibt es bestimmte Berührungsängste vielleicht weniger als mit der Molekularbiologie oder der Quantenphysik. Politik- und Sozialwissenschaften liegen irgendwo dazwischen. Natürlich hängt das auch davon ab, welche Berührungspunkte man selbst mit den entsprechenden Disziplinen hat. Und wir können beobachten, dass sich das auch verändert. Zum Beispiel in der Corona-Pandemie, als Fachbegriffe aus der Virologie und Epidemiologie plötzlich Einzug in alltägliche Gespräche gehalten haben.

Verschiedene Disziplinen erfordern in der Kommunikation auch unterschiedliche Ansätze. Die sozialwissenschaftlichen Themen muss man manchmal stärker von der alltäglichen Betrachtung wegrücken. Es liegt eine besondere Herausforderung darin, nicht nur zu vermitteln, was die Ergebnisse der Forschung in diesen Bereichen sind, sondern auch zu verdeutlichen: Was können Wissenschaftler*innen zu diesem Thema sagen, was ich als eine Person, die einfach nur Nachrichten schaut, dazu nicht sagen kann? Es geht also auch darum, bei unserem Zielpublikum eine gewisse Scientific Literacy mit aufzubauen. Auf der anderen Seite kann es im naturwissenschaftlichen Bereich wichtiger sein, die Themen näher an die Leute heranzurücken und vom Fachjargon in etwas zu übersetzen, woran sie anknüpfen können.

[Sicherheit & Innovation Alle Beiträge zum Jahresfokus](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/schwerpunkt-sicherheit-innovation/)

Die Interdisziplinarität erfordert dann, diese Ansätze zusammenzubringen. Wir reden gerade ganz allgemein von Wissenschaftskommunikation, aber wir haben natürlich unterschiedliche Zielgruppen, und die haben unterschiedliche Kenntnisstände. Es ist wichtig, sich das bewusst zu machen und eine Art modularen Ansatz zu wählen. Wir überlegen: Was sind die wichtigsten Kernbotschaften? Welche Hintergrundinformationen könnte eine Person brauchen, die nicht im Thema drin ist? Wie können wir visuelle Elemente einsetzen, um die Zugänglichkeit der Themen zu erhöhen?

**Wissenschaft sollte möglichst offen und transparent sein. Wenn es um sicherheitsrelevante Forschung geht, kann Transparenz jedoch auch Risiken bergen. Wo verläuft da die Grenze zwischen Offenheit und verantwortungsvollem Schutz?**

Das ist immer eine Abwägung im Einzelfall. Ich denke, die eigentliche, schwierigere Frage findet nicht erst in der Kommunikation statt, sondern schon früher. Bei einem großen Risikopotenzial ist die Frage grundlegend: Was kann ich davon überhaupt veröffentlichen?

Eine mögliche Maßnahme ist, nur einen Teil der Forschungsergebnisse in einem Journal zu veröffentlichen. Das beißt sich natürlich damit, wie Wissenschaft überhaupt funktioniert. Sie ist eigentlich auf Reproduzierbarkeit, Offenheit und Dialog angelegt. Die Wissenschaftskommunikation kann sich hier nicht gänzlich aus der Affäre ziehen. Allerdings denke ich, dass wir nicht diejenigen sind, die solche Abwägungen treffen können, weil sie selbst Gegenstand einer wissenschaftlichen Einschätzung sind.

Die Kommunikation sicherheitsrelevanter Themen hat jedoch selbst eine sicherheitsrelevante Komponente. Denn dadurch, dass man sagt: „Achtung, diese Forschung ließe sich missbrauchen auf diese und jene Art und Weise“, erzeugt man auch die Gefahr, dass man die Aufmerksamkeit auf das Missbrauchspotenzial lenkt. Auch wir Kommunikator*innen, die Aufmerksamkeit lenken wollen, müssen also umsichtig vorgehen.

articleBody:
### “Third things are essential to marriages, objects or practices or habits or arts or institutions or games or human beings that provide a site of joint rapture or contentment.”

“The encounter between two differences is an event,” French philosopher Alain Badiou wrote in his tremendous treatise on [why we fall and how we stay in love](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/10/26/alain-badiou-in-praise-of-love/). “On the basis of this event, love can start and flourish. It is the first, absolutely essential point.”

And yet at the heart of this essential event is often something beyond the two — something often improbable, almost always inessential in itself, which somehow magnetizes the two differences into a unit of belonging.

The power of that mysterious and magical something is what the poet and essayist **Donald Hall** (September 20, 1928–June 23, 2018) explores in a gorgeous essay titled “The Third Thing,” which appeared on the pages of [Poetry](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine) — the world’s most enduring and visionary poetry magazine — in the autumn of 2004.

Donald Hall and Jane Kenyon

Reflecting on his life with the love of his life — the poet Jane Kenyon, herself the keeper and giver of [uncommonly clarifying wisdom on writing and life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/09/15/jane-kenyon-advice-on-writing/) — Hall considers the secret to the kind of lasting love that blooms between the mundane and the magical. An epoch after Virginia Woolf exulted in [“the bead of sensation”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/05/11/virginia-woolf-on-relationships-marriage/) that punctuates the dailiness of any durational love to make it last, Hall writes:

> Jane Kenyon and I were married for twenty-three years. For two decades we inhabited the double solitude of my family farmhouse in New Hampshire, writing poems, loving the countryside. She was forty-seven when she died. If anyone had asked us, “Which year was the best, of your lives together?” we could have agreed on an answer: “the one we remember least.” There were sorrowful years — the death of her father, my cancers, her depressions — and there were also years of adventure: a trip to China and Japan, two trips to India; years when my children married; years when the grandchildren were born; years of triumph as Jane began her public life in poetry: her first book, her first poem in the New Yorker. The best moment of our lives was one quiet repeated day of work in our house. Not everyone understood. Visitors, especially from New York, would spend a weekend with us and say as they left: “It’s really pretty here” (“in Vermont,” many added) “with your house, the pond, the hills, but … but … but … what do you do? ”
> What we did: we got up early in the morning. I brought Jane coffee in bed. She walked the dog as I started writing, then climbed the stairs to work at her own desk on her own poems. We had lunch. We lay down together. We rose and worked at secondary things. I read aloud to Jane; we played scoreless ping-pong; we read the mail; we worked again. We ate supper, talked, read books sitting across from each other in the living room, and went to sleep. If we were lucky the phone didn’t ring all day… Three hundred and thirty days a year we inhabited this old house and the same day’s adventurous routine.
> What we did: love.

Art from [The Missing Piece Meets the Big O](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/02/12/the-missing-piece-meets-the-big-o-shel-silverstein/) — Shel Silverstein’s allegory of the secret to lasting love

But the substance of this daily love, Hall argues, is not the stuff of romantic tropes. Echoing *Little Prince* author Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s [beautiful insistence](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/01/01/what-is-love/) that “love does not consist of gazing at each other, but in looking outward together in the same direction,” Hall writes:

> We did not spend our days gazing into each other’s eyes. We did that gazing when we made love or when one of us was in trouble, but most of the time our gazes met and entwined as they looked at a third thing. Third things are essential to marriages, objects or practices or habits or arts or institutions or games or human beings that provide a site of joint rapture or contentment. Each member of a couple is separate; the two come together in double attention. Lovemaking is not a third thing but two-in-one. John Keats can be a third thing, or the Boston Symphony Orchestra, or Dutch interiors, or Monopoly.

Art by Sophie Blackall from [Things to Look Forward to](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/05/12/sophie-blackall-things-to-look-forward-to/)

For Hall and Kenyon, the third thing was the pond near their home. He writes:

> We had our summer afternoons at the pond, which for ten years made a third thing. After naps we loaded up books and blankets and walked across Route 4 and the old railroad to the steep slippery bank that led down to our private beach on Eagle Pond. Soft moss underfoot sent little red flowers up. Ghost birches leaned over water with wild strawberry plants growing under them. Over our heads white pines reared high, and oaks that warned us of summer’s end late in August by dropping green metallic acorns. Sometimes a mink scooted among ferns… Jane dozed in the sun as I sat in the shade reading and occasionally taking a note in a blank book. From time to time we swam and dried in the heat.

Hall’s most piercing point is that the third thing, rather than being an extraneous adornment of the relationship, is a central form of companionship. But while it is indispensable, it is not irreplaceable — it doesn’t so much matter what the thing is, only that it is.

Art by Maira Kalman from [Achieving Perspective](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/02/18/achieving-perspective/) for [The Universe in Verse](https://www.themarginalian.org/the-universe-in-verse/)

When a landfill leakage destroyed their beloved pond, Hall and Kenyon still had their other third thing — poetry. Reflecting on its [unparalleled power of perspective](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/02/18/achieving-perspective/), its power to connect and console in the face of life’s darkest moments, he writes:

> We lived in the house of poetry, which was also the house of love and grief; the house of solitude and art; the house of Jane’s depression and my cancers and Jane’s leukemia. When someone died whom we loved, we went back to the poets of grief and outrage, as far back as Gilgamesh; often I read aloud Henry King’s “The Exequy,” written in the seventeenth century after the death of his young wife. Poetry gives the griever not release from grief but companionship in grief. Poetry embodies the complexities of feeling at their most intense and entangled, and therefore offers (over centuries, or over no time at all) the company of tears. As I sat beside Jane in her pain and weakness I wrote about pain and weakness. Once in a hospital I noticed that the leaves were turning. I realized that I had not noticed that they had come to the trees. It was a year without seasons, a year without punctuation. I began to write “Without” to embody the sensations of lives under dreary, monotonous assault. After I had drafted it many times I read it aloud to Jane. “That’s it, Perkins,” she said. “You’ve got it. That’s it.” Even in this poem written at her mortal bedside there was companionship.

Hall’s 1999 poetry collection [Without](http://www.amazon.com/Without-Poems-Donald-Hall/dp/0395957656/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](http://www.worldcat.org/title/without-poems/oclc/37579932&referer=brief_results)) is the breathtakingly beautiful record of that abiding companionship. Complement it with Anna Dostoyevskaya on [the secret to a happy marriage](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/02/15/anna-dostoyevsky-reminiscences-marriage/) and Wendell Berry on [what poetry teaches us about the secret of marriage](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/11/18/wendell-berry-poetry-marriage/) and Adrienne Rich on [honorable human relationships](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/07/02/adrienne-rich-honorable-human-relationship/).

### donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing *The Marginalian* (which [bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/22/brain-pickings-becoming-the-marginalian/) for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a [donation](https://www.themarginalian.org/donate/). Your support makes all the difference.

### newsletter

*The Marginalian* has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s [what to expect](https://mailchi.mp/brainpickings/janna-levin-rebecca-elson-anne-lamott-james-gleick). Like? [Sign up.](https://www.themarginalian.org/newsletter/)

The power of that mysterious and magical something is what the poet and essayist Donald Hall (September 20, 1928–June 23, 2018) explores in a gorgeous essay titled “The Third Thing,” which appea…

title: When Your Doctor Prescribes a Visit to an Art Gallery

articleBody:
The soulful deep greens and browns of British Columbia’s forests weave together with ferns and moss, catching the light through the tops of ancient firs and cedars. The trees sway, and the earth rises and falls among the rocks.

But in this case, the view isn’t from the trail. It is a painting by Canadian artist Emily Carr on display in the [Vancouver Art Gallery](https://www.vanartgallery.bc.ca/art-of-wellbeing/), and some of those who are experiencing it are doing so because it was prescribed by their health care provider. How they ended up there is the result of a bit of creative thinking that honors the role of art in healing.

In 2025, the gallery partnered with BC Parks Foundation to extend [PaRx](https://www.parkprescriptions.ca/), Canada’s national nature prescription program, to include the gallery. PaRx is a successful initiative that has included an estimated 2 million prescriptions issued by more than 20,000 health care providers. Typically, these prescriptions are for time outdoors, with added benefits, like free transportation, to reduce barriers to access.

Using art as an entry point into nature as a formal intervention is novel—the first collaboration of its kind between a nature prescription program and an arts institution in the world, according to Sirish Rao, the gallery’s co-CEO and executive director. While art-based prescriptions are gaining in popularity, this program goes a step further, integrating engagement with nature in a gentle, accessible way. Other institutions around the world are looking to the Vancouver Art Gallery program as a model initiative that can be replicated in other communities to support people’s well-being.

*Credit: Vancouver Art Gallery*

## An artful approach to treatment

The process starts when a health care provider like a doctor, nurse, or therapist determines that a patient might benefit from a prescription to spend time in nature, including around the nature-inspired visual art at the gallery. The benefits can be many: combating isolation, engaging mentally and physically during a gallery visit, and experiencing awe and beauty.

The prescription to Vancouver Art Gallery includes free admission for the prescription holder and a guest, as well as a printed guide that offers prompts and questions to consider—for example, to notice the varied shades of green Carr used, or imagine a walk along a trail she painted—along with research about the benefits of experiencing nature. Participants are guided through “slow looking” as the act of learning through observation, imagination exercises, and physical movement—yes, swaying in an art gallery is encouraged.

After the visit, guests are invited to continue the immersion at a local nature space, with free carshare minutes to get there if needed. The art prescription guide suggests nearby parks where participants can walk or hike, extending slow looking from a curated indoor experience to the outdoors if they choose. And they can return to the gallery as often as they like by retaining their original prescription. On site, they can join free workshops, and a coloring book offers a contemplative experience at home.

This is an example of social prescribing, a worldwide movement that serves as a complement to clinical care and typical medication prescriptions by prescribing from a wide range of activities that support physical and mental health. Beyond art galleries and nature walks, this can include music classes, exercise sessions, or gardening programs. The prescription is personal and can be tailored to patients’ needs and interests.

Carla Fry is a West Vancouver psychologist and educator with more than 20 years of clinical experience. She says the art gallery prescription has been a gift for participants, especially those who face physical, mental, social, or even financial or transportation barriers to accessing nature. Many are surprised that they don’t have to pay anything for the experience.

“For them to understand that so many people have come together to create this opportunity, I think that in and of itself is special,” Fry says. “They say, ‘Wow, my community cares.’ The possibility that this exists, it’s available, it’s free—there’s something about that... that’s noteworthy.”

Fry is one of the professionals who gives these kinds of prescriptions to her clients. It’s another tool available to promote well-being.

“Of course, I’m never telling them to go. We talk about this as a prescription, but I always present it as ‘here’s an opportunity to meet some of your goals, and here’s what the opportunity looks like,’” she says.

As yet, no one has declined her prescription.

“They’re surprised that something so seemingly simplistic as slowing down and really looking, really living in front of the art or in nature is actually an intervention,” Fry says. “People in our culture are set up to think that growth has got to be painful, growth has got to be difficult, growth has got to be expensive, growth is going to take a long time. When I bring forward an intervention of going to a location, and your job as a client of mine is to appreciate, the first reaction is surprise. It opens up an entire conversation—‘I can just appreciate my life and not always be grinding to make it better.’ It’s a special process for me to witness.”

## Awe and nature in community

The goal is to do more than increase the number of people who have exposure to art, though that might be a side effect. The formal prescription to nature through art is designed to reduce stress, anxiety, and social isolation. The ability to bring a guest, as well as the opportunity to experience art with other patrons, is key.

“There are other people there; these aren’t private viewings. But of course, sometimes people don’t feel connected to others in a room. Sometimes they do; sometimes it’s enough to feel that they’re part of a community. But others really benefit from being able to have a shared experience where they can reflect in real time and reflect afterwards,” Fry says.

Paula Toledo is the mental health advisor and lead well-being consultant at Vancouver Art Gallery, leading the [Richardson Family Art of Wellbeing Lab](https://www.vanartgallery.bc.ca/art-of-wellbeing/). The lab aims to connect the community to art as a means to improve mental and physical well-being, drawing on a collaboration of researchers, scientists, physicians, and Indigenous Elders and healers.

Toledo came to this work through the personal experience of losing her husband and her mother within months, while also caring for her newborn child. That grief and her recovery changed the course of her life and her career in wellness.

“When we encounter something so vast that it transcends our current understanding of the world, it can be very mysterious,” Toledo says:

> Sometimes it can be a very positive experience, but other times, like in cases of grief, it can also make you stop and wonder about the mystery behind it. I was in awe and I remember that exact moment where I thought, “Well, if that could happen, then the opposite must also be true.” That’s what the research supports: When we experience awe, it can lead to wonder, which is this mental state of openness and curiosity. Every day I woke up with that sense of curiosity that this might be the day that I turn the corner and collide with good fortune. That experience was so transformative that it led me to actually seek out resources.

Toledo’s health care provider connected her with a social worker who prescribed movement and art in the form of yoga and music classes.

I started to feel more energized and connected to my own self-determination,” she says. “If we look at the research on why social prescribing is so impactful, it’s because it really does encourage self-determination. I started to feel more connected to my community, more connected to my children, connecting to their own wonder, and it became this upward spiral towards healing and towards rebuilding my life.”

## Art by prescription

Monica Harrison is one of the many prescription holders who has learned to lean into the peace and beauty of slowing down through the program. She is an educational assistant who works with students with support needs and advocates for their inclusion in schools. She experienced health issues that required her to be on leave from work and that triggered depression and anxiety.

“I’m neurodivergent, so I’m autistic and I have ADHD. I’ve had anxiety my whole life, and I’ve learned a lot of coping mechanisms that help me to control that. But with undiagnosed conditions that have been going on, it has awoken a lot of anxiety, and it makes it hard to manage my mood,” she says.

Harrison met Toledo, who introduced her to the prescription program. What started with Harrison’s immersion in art has resulted in her increasing use of the program in other locations, both indoors and out.

Harrison, who enjoys nature photography, says she was introduced to Carr’s paintings in elementary school, and she fell in love with the local subject matter. Now as an adult, that connection to art has opened new opportunities.

“When we visited the gallery, I was able to discuss paintings and identify what I was feeling. It really allowed me to label what I was feeling more accurately and then think about it. Just through her artwork, it really made me feel nurturing and protection,” she says.

Through other exhibitions at the gallery, Harrison says she found surprise and joy and “a lot of beautiful sensory feelings to my mind and my body and my soul”:

> Chronic illnesses [have] made my life very small, with a lot of losses that come with the territory, such as giving up things that I once enjoyed like working, walking in nature, seeing friends, traveling. I found the prescription to be very flexible. You can do it whenever you’re able to. It can give you something specific to try out. You can do it on your own. You can do it with friends and family, and I think it’s a great thing for people with chronic illness. And it can also give those people a practical way to learn how nature connects to positive mental health. It can be something they can build on through a positive experience with their prescription... and add to their toolkit.

Fry says she hears two recurring themes from prescription holders: Experiencing art feels immersive, and the process of visiting the gallery—from the prescription as an invitation to the encouragement to engage in “slow looking”—is a special event that makes them feel cared for.

“It’s something different. It’s something novel. It’s something fresh,” she says, whereas doing the same gratitude practices over and over can get repetitive. “It’s a lot more powerful when we add novel opportunities or events or experiences to our practice. For every person that I’ve prescribed this to, it’s been new to them, so it hits that mark really nicely,” she says.

## A new, slow way of seeing

Art, nature, music, dance, and other social prescriptions have decades of demonstrated success. Toledo points to social prescribing in the U.K. as an example where community connectors or social workers serve as entry points for patients to discover what activities might be meaningful to them. For some, that might mean a return to an activity they enjoyed in years past, like Toledo’s own reengagement with music during her grief.

The social prescription movement continues to gain ground, with providers taking notice at a growing pace. It requires community, collaboration, and a foundation of care that looks at health through a wide lens. In the United States, organizations like Social Prescribing USA are championing the effort as a medical intervention.

For Rao, the impact extends far beyond people’s visits to the gallery.

“What we’re looking at is a way of seeing,” Rao says. “That way of seeing then applies to anything.”

title: Mindful Eating
subtitle: This food reveals your connection with the Earth.
feedText: With mindfulness we can see that many elements—the rain, sunshine, earth, and the labor of the farmers, drivers, food sellers, and cook—have all come together to form each wonderful meal. When we eat in mindfulness, we can see that the entire universe is supporting our existence. Having the opportunity to sit and enjoy a wonderful meal is something precious, something not everyone has. Many people in the world are hungry. articleBody:
Mindful eating is an important part of our meditation practice—from chopping vegetables to eating with awareness to cleaning up. With [mindfulness](http://google.com/url?q=https://tricycle.org/buddhism-misunderstandings/%23mindfulness-primary-practice&sa=D&source=editors&ust=1794344459664192&usg=AOvVaw3noZmbxwjn3sqon9r8wjed) we can see that many elements—the rain, sunshine, earth, and the labor of the farmers, drivers, food sellers, and cook—have all come together to form each wonderful meal. When we eat in mindfulness, we can see that the entire universe is supporting our existence.

Having the opportunity to sit and enjoy a wonderful meal is something precious, something not everyone has. Many people in the world are hungry. When I hold a bowl of rice or a piece of bread, I know that I am fortunate, and I feel [compassion](https://tricycle.org/tag/compassion-karuna/) for all those who have no food to eat or who are without friends or family. We can be aware of this right at our dinner table. Mindful eating can cultivate seeds of compassion and understanding. Those seeds can sprout and grow inside us and give us the determination to do something to help hungry and lonely people to be nourished.

The kitchen should be a place of meditation. You might want to create a kitchen altar to remind yourself to practice mindfulness while cooking. It can be just a small shelf with enough room for an incense holder, a small flower vase, a beautiful stone, a small picture of an ancestor or a spiritual teacher, or a statue of the Buddha or a [bodhisattva](https://tricycle.org/glossary/bodhisattva/)—whatever is most meaningful to you. When you come into the kitchen, you can begin your work by offering incense and practicing mindful breathing.

While cooking, allow enough time so you don’t feel rushed. Be aware that you, and the people you’re cooking for, depend on this food. This awareness will help you to cook healthy food that’s infused with your love and mindfulness.

When the food is on the table and everyone is seated, practice at least three mindful breaths before beginning to eat. You can say:

*Breathing in, I calm my body.* *Breathing out, I smile.*

If you’re eating alone, promise yourself just to eat and to be with the food, and not to read or listen to the radio or watch a screen during the meal. If you’re eating with others, take the time to really look at each of them and smile. Sitting at the table with other people is a chance to offer an authentic smile of friendship and understanding. It’s very easy, but not many people do it. To me, the most important part of the practice is to look at each person and smile. If people eating together cannot smile at each other, then something isn’t right.

After breathing and smiling, look down at the food in a way that allows it to become real. This food reveals your connection with the Earth. Each bite contains the life of the sun and the Earth. The extent to which your food reveals itself depends on you. You can see and taste the whole universe in a piece of bread!

Contemplating your food for a few seconds before eating, and eating in mindfulness, can bring you much happiness. You can say:

*In this food* *I see clearly the presence* *of the entire universe* *supporting my existence.*

When you’ve finished eating, take a few moments to notice that your bowl or plate is now empty and your hunger is satisfied. You can take a moment to be grateful that you have had this nourishing food to eat, supporting you on the path of love and understanding, by saying:

*The plate is empty.* *My hunger is satisfied.* *I vow to live* *for the benefit of all beings.*

When you’re cleaning the kitchen or [washing dishes](https://tricycle.org/magazine/wash-your-bowl/), do it as if you were washing a baby, and you can feel joy and peace radiate within and around you. You can say to yourself:

*Washing the dishes* *is like bathing a baby.* *The profane is the sacred.* *Everyday mind is enlightened mind.*

From time to time, you might want to try the practice of eating in silence, even if you’re eating with family or friends. Eating in silence allows us to see the preciousness of the food and our friends, as well as our close relationship with the Earth and all species. Every vegetable, every drop of water, every piece of bread contains in it the life of our planet and the whole cosmos. With each bite of food, we can taste the meaning and value of our life.

## A Recipe from Plum Village: Tender Sweet Potatoes

Seven years before founding Plum Village in southwest France, Thích Nhất Hạnh and Sister Chân Không established a community near Paris named after this humble and delicious vegetable. In her autobiography, *Learning True Love*, Sister Chân Không writes, “In 1975, [we] moved with several friends to a house near Fontannes, France. The war in Vietnam had ended and we were cut off from our country with no way to help. We named our community Les Patates Douces, or Sweet Potatoes. In Vietnam, when peasants have no rice, they eat dried sweet potatoes. It is the poorest food, and we knew we needed some way to be in touch with the poorest people in our country. Thanks to that house and land, we were able to heal some of our wounds and appreciate the beauties of France.” Now in Plum Village, we eat sweet potatoes in a variety of ways—baked, mashed, and even boiled—and we no longer think of it as a poor person’s food. You can try cooking root vegetables such as parsnips, turnips, or rutabagas (swedes) in the same minimalist way. Roasting vegetables a little longer than expected, until lightly caramelized, deepens their natural sweetness and means almost no seasoning is needed. In Plum Village meals, their sweetness and vibrant colors balance salty main dishes and green veggies.

*Makes 2–4 servings*

**2–3 sweet potatoes** **1–2 tbsp olive oil** **½ tsp salt** **black pepper (optional)**

Preheat the oven to 400°F (200°C).

Wash the sweet potatoes and remove any roots or damaged areas.

Based on the shape of the sweet potato, cut into shapes that will allow the most uniform cooking—cubes, thick round slices, or long wedges—leaving the skins on for extra color and nutrition.

Place the pieces on a baking tray and toss with the olive oil, salt, and black pepper. Spread the sweet potatoes in one single layer.

Bake for 25–35 minutes. Halfway through baking, turn the pieces so that both sides caramelize.

The sweet potatoes are ready when they are very soft inside and the edges are golden brown and slightly crisp.

♦

*From* [The Plum Village Cookbook: Simple Plant-Based Recipes for Mindful Living from the Zen Monastery of Thich Nhat Hanh](https://www.parallax.org/product/the-plum-village-cookbook/) *. Reprinted with permission from Parallax Press, www.parallax.org.*

#### Did You Know?

Winslow Homer's studio in Prouts Neck, Maine, is a National Historic Landmark.

### Description

The powerful Atlantic surf pounding against the desolate coast of Prouts Neck, Maine, provided primary subject matter for the dramatic paintings that Homer created during his final decades. This example, which the artist proclaimed as "the best picture of the sea that I have painted," was initially conceived as a watercolor. Undertaking the composition in oil after a lapse of nearly two decades, Homer patiently waited for the appropriate atmospheric conditions, executing the work in four different sessions spread over two years.

articleBody:
# Hiring a Systems Programmer for Boxem | Lobsters

### Hiring a Systems Programmer for Boxem

- job
authored byabnercoimbre2026-11-19 10:45:34 | 12 comments | +26, 12 off-topic

Handmade Cities has a job referral program, where engineers and employers reach out about open roles. (It's a free community service, so I'm not getting paid.)

I'm cross-posting an unusually good opportunity from Boxem, who are writing fast shipping software and are very keen to hire a veteran C programmer:

"You will program in C and compile to linux and WASM. Linux nonblocking socket servers and WASM UI apps with modern graphics drivers. Custom versioned databases written to fit exactly the task. Write from scratch to reduce volume of code and complexity."

Few more notes:

- Boxem's remote for now, but will open a Miami office Q2 2027, after which they'll pay for your relocation.
- You may apply online already. Application includes salary bands and rest of the info you need
- I know the CEO so I've invited them to Lobsters. Ask any questions for the next number of days and they'll respond here!
- 18WilhelmVonWeiner2026-11-19 23:21:57
Boxem's remote for now, but will open a Miami office Q2 2027, after which they'll pay for your relocation.

Downgrading like that is crazy.

- 3ghthor2026-11-20 07:37:10
Yeah, that’s an awful downgrade.

- 19abnercoimbre2026-11-19 11:03:11
Did I miss something about the rules of Lobsters? (Seeing as this got flagged off-topic by a user.) The jobs tag reads as:

Employment/Internship opportunities

This is an employment opportunity I wanted to elevate, because it's rare to know a CEO looking to hire a low-level programmer and wants you writing code from scratch.

- 11355E3BSysop2026-11-19 12:35:29
We've generally done these kinds of posts in a shared quarterly thread with a fixed format.

- 12ile-du-fantome edited 2026-11-19 13:39:33
That doesn't seem like a valid reason for people to flag this as "off topic". I hope you or another moderator will do the competent thing and remove those flags.

- 17icefox2026-11-19 17:27:19
Jeez, chill.

- 3ile-du-fantome2026-11-20 00:51:13
Yeah, alright, I've been disappointed with how Lobsters has been ran for, well to be honest, forever, but the past few months especially, and that bled into my comment here. My bad.

- 4proctrap2026-11-19 22:47:25
you or another moderator will do the competent thing

Uh that reads very close to "you or another competent moderator" as in: you judge what is the competent thing to do as a moderator. I do not believe removing flags is normally done at all.

- 8luke80862026-11-20 01:38:25
Pick an animal you feel best represents you and explain why

WTF, I thought it was a running joke. Are companies doing it for real?

- 1proctrap2026-11-21 22:56:08
There is only one true answer: Chimeric Slime, obviously. Can shapeshift into anything, can't get hit as it's just a slime and can absorb anything. I hope that enlightened the interviewer.

- 2eldondev2026-11-19 18:23:00
Seems like an interesting opportunity, but details are so sparse, C still strikes me as a strange choice for these targets, and being at the whim of Amazon sounds less than appealing. Probably a solid business, though.

- 6calvin2026-11-20 08:33:00
Yeah, for greenfield high-performance stuff, C when you're just targeting modern WebAssembly and Linux is strange when Rust or Zig exist depending on your preferences. Even modern C++ would have made more sense.

title: Born Erased ~ What You Destroy, I Love
subtitle: Born Erased brings together two sides of Bulgarian musician Angel Simitchiev’s musical practice: the dark ambient experimentation of his former sol…
feedText: But it’s a relief.” His third outing as Born Erased, What You Destroy, I Love, revisits the concrete angst of his 2023 debut, I Am the End of the World, with a heavier emphasis on guitars and live percussion. There’s even a touch of colour, at least in Silvana Ilieva’s artwork, which resembles molten lava flowing beneath the earth’s surface. Simitchiev, however, offers no soothing remedy for the world’s ailments. Written in response to the seemingly endless cycle of wars, human suffering and environmental destru…
articleBody:
**Born Erased** brings together two sides of Bulgarian musician Angel Simitchiev’s musical practice: the dark ambient experimentation of his former solo project Mytrip and the harsher sounds of Dayin, which he once described as “Harsh drones and regret. But it’s a relief.” His third outing as Born Erased, *What You Destroy, I Love*, revisits the concrete angst of his 2023 debut, *I Am the End of the World*, with a heavier emphasis on guitars and live percussion. There’s even a touch of colour, at least in Silvana Ilieva’s artwork, which resembles molten lava flowing beneath the earth’s surface.

Simitchiev, however, offers no soothing remedy for the world’s ailments. Written in response to the seemingly endless cycle of wars, human suffering and environmental destruction, the album is an expression of anger at humanity’s willingness to sacrifice life and the natural world in pursuit of power and profit. The opening “Knife Hands” establishes the mood with crushing drones that ebb and flow beneath skies already blackened by an unrelenting darkness, like ink rapidly spreading across watercolour paper. “Sea of Skin” begins with a low rumble from the earth’s core before erupting into post-rock territory, propelled by drums and distorted guitars.

As Simitchiev explains in the accompanying interview, the compositions began as ambient pieces, with drummer Nedislav Miladinov invited to respond freely to their atmosphere. Only afterwards did Simitchiev write the guitar and bass parts around the recorded drums. This approach accounts for some of the music’s unpredictable momentum, as the pieces expand and contract under their own considerable weight.

On “Diamond Silence”, the magmatic force reaches the surface, accompanied by the ghostly vocals of Romain Barbot of Saåad, whose fragile presence offers a rare moment of intimacy. “Like Wraiths” takes us across scorched earth, while “The Last Embrace” moves through coruscating textures, with Siavash Amini contributing additional layers of noise and disquiet.

“Unbelonging” retreats into more familiar dark ambient territory, its steady drumming offering a deceptive sense of reassurance as sweeping, glacial drones clear the horizon of any remaining sonic debris. The piece eventually erupts into a volcanic torrent of distortion, dispelling any illusion of safety. It’s this false familiarity that makes the album so unsettling: just when the music seems to offer some respite, the ground gives way again.

The closing “A Future Without the Body” abandons all hope of salvation. Its thrusting, strident passages seem intent on stripping away the last remnants of humanity before gradually dissipating into thin air. The silence left in their wake is all the more powerful.

*What You Destroy, I Love* offers little prospect of redemption. Simitchiev’s anger is directed not at the natural world but at humanity’s determination to destroy it, along with itself. If there is any hope remaining, it lies in the possibility that the planet might eventually reclaim what we have so recklessly squandered.

Born Erased live by Niya Kirkova

To uncover the different layers of the production process I have reached out directly to [Angel Simitchiev](https://linktr.ee/angelxsimitchiev).

**What You Destroy, I Love sounds considerably heavier than [Birds Drink My Blood](https://bornerased.bandcamp.com/album/birds-drink-my-blood), with elements of shoegaze and post-rock. In some ways, it feels closer to your debut, [I Am the End of the World](https://bornerased.bandcamp.com/album/i-am-the-end-of-the-world), which drew on your background in hardcore punk. Was this a conscious return to that sound? And how much did Nedislav Miladinov’s drumming influence the direction of the album?**

The new record is certainly heavier and closer to the music of the debut full-length; it was actually written and recorded right after I released *I Am the End of the World*. However, the production took longer than I expected for multiple reasons, and while waiting for everything to be ready – meaning guest features, mixing, mastering, artwork – I took a little detour from this heavier, guitar- and live drums-oriented sound and made *Birds Drink My Blood*, which sounds closer to what I was doing with my previous, and now defunct, solo project Mytrip or what I’ve been releasing under the name [Dayin](https://dayin.bandcamp.com/).

Nedislav Miladinov’s drums on the record definitely impacted the way the tracks moved forward. Just like the first album, I would build a solely ambient skeleton of a piece, then I would ask the drummer to interpret it without guiding them too much or expecting any particular drum part or pattern to be played. Once the drums have been tracked, I’d write the guitar and bass parts based on wherever the drums took the music. So, without the drums, these tracks would’ve been something entirely different. It’s a challenging process for a drummer because we don’t use click tracks; you can’t really count anything in these first bits you’re playing over, you have no other choice but just let the atmosphere guide you.

**You’ve worked with quite a few musicians on your Born Erased albums, including Mondkopf, Vanity Productions and Moss Harvest. This time you’ve brought in Romain Barbot of Saåad on “Diamond Silence” and Siavash Amini on “The Last Embrace”. How did you get to know them, and what made you want to work together? Did you give them much freedom with their contributions, or did you already have a clear idea of what you wanted?**

Collaboration is the main thing that differentiates Born Erased from any of my previous solo projects. I’ve spent so much time making electronic and experimental music alone while simultaneously playing in hardcore punk bands; I wanted to bring a little bit of this dynamic to the other side of my musical practice. As I like to say, I wanted to leave the door open for other people’s ideas, and so far in these three albums I’ve managed to work with people whose music I truly admire, and who are all around great. By no means do I suggest what any of the guest musicians is expected to do on a track I’ve invited them on. I know their music and trust their understanding of what I do, and so far each collaboration has always been successful.

Saåad is one of my all-time favorite projects. I love and have all of their records, and throughout the years I’ve kept in touch with Romain. He was one of the first people to listen to *I Am The End of the World*, and ended up releasing it on his label BLWBCK. Saåad’s contribution to the album was a true blessing, as Romain actually added his vocals to the track, making it such an intimate, fragile, and special part of a record that is so heavy and aggressive. As for Siavash, I’m a big fan of his music as well; I love his more academic and technological approach to sound and composition, which results in these complex, abrasive but very musical soundscapes… It’s just so inspiring. He’s living in Iran, and I’m grateful he found the time and motivation to share his unique approach with me during some of the most difficult times in his life. I’ll never forget this.

**I’m curious about the title What You Destroy, I Love. It sounds almost like an accusation. Is it directed at anyone or anything in particular? And is there a connection between the title and tracks such as “Knife Hands”, “Unbelonging” and “A Future Without the Body”?**

These tracks you mention are certainly connected, but all tracks on the album are parts of an inseparable whole. When we play them live, they fit perfectly with the material from *I Am the End of the World,* so I believe the connection runs even deeper and will continue to expand with each new record.

At its core, *What You Destroy, I Love* is an anti-violence album. I’m so fed up with living in a world constantly being at war; I’m so fed up with waking up and seeing the horrors taking place in Palestine, Lebanon, Iran, Ukraine, and Sudan, to name a few… These atrocities are basically everywhere. It’s my reaction against everyone willing to sacrifice not only the lives of thousands of innocent people but also destroy the planet in the process. And we all know it’s for greed, for money, power, and territories. Things that won’t matter when we’re all dead. It’s like we are reliving the first 50 years of the 20th century, but now we see it in real-time, on our phones, on a daily basis. I despise everyone supporting and justifying war or any kind of violence in the year 2026.

**I was reading the liner notes for I Am the End of the World, where you talk about anger and hatred towards the world, but also the hope of finding freedom, even if it means destroying the reality we’re forced to live in. Do you still feel that way? The new album was recorded between 2023 and 2024, so I’m also wondering whether your feelings about the music have changed since then.**

It’s been two years since I wrote and recorded the music on *What You Destroy, I Love*, and not only haven’t I changed my mind, I’m even more convinced we’re on the wrong path. But like it or not, the world as we know it will probably end up being torn to pieces. I just hope nature will do its job and shake us off its back before we nuke everything dead. I believe only when humanity hits rock bottom will it have the chance to actually evolve and rebel against its primal instincts, to conquer and destroy everything it touches instead of living in peace with the world we’ve been so generously gifted. Until we learn to co-exist instead of exploit, everything will get worse and worse. The only thing that has a chance of humbling us as a species is, I believe, a bigger force stepping in. Thankfully, the planet has a lot of those at hand.

( **Gianmarco Del Re** )

articleBody:
# Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon

Back to Articles

## Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon

TeamArticlePublished November 26, 2026 Upvote 34

angtangtggml-orgSimon Pagezypagezyhfggml-orgAbdennacer Badaouibadaouiggml-org

The llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware.

Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance.

### Quick start

You can choose Hardware, Model, and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201).

- In the Overview tab, compare quantizations for one hardware, model, and build. The two charts show PP512 (512 input tokens, no generation) and TG128 (128 generated tokens), both starting at context depth zero.
- In the Build history tab, track PP512 and TG128 across all recorded builds for the selected hardware, model, and quantization.
- In the Contextscaling tab, see how token-generation throughput changes as the existing context grows, for the selected build, hardware, model, and quantization.
### What the numbers mean

The dashboard shows two separate tests, both measured in tokens per second:

TestWorkloadWhat it helps you assessPP512Process 512 input tokensHow quickly the model processes a promptTG128Generate 128 tokensHow quickly the model produces output

Both tests start at context depth zero (n_depth=0). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput (avg_ts). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows.

### How we run the benchmarks

We benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh, the build and installation project behind llama.app. The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration.

The model set evolves and currently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M, Q8_0, other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16.

### Inspect and reuse the results

The explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model.

Standard results use <build>/<hardware>/<model>/<quant>.jsonl. Workload sweeps use the same folder <quant>-tg.jsonl filename.

Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run.

### Join the conversation

Thanks to the AMD team for providing test infrastructure and helping validate the setup! Try the dashboard, inspect the data, and let us know which models and workloads you would like to see next.

feedText: # The gentle sounds of a tiny acoustic piano from Denmark - CDM Create Digital Music MusicMusic techTech ## The gentle sounds of a tiny acoustic piano from Denmark Peter Kirn - November 25, 2026 Add comment In northern Europe, it’s that time of year that disappears under a thick blanket of cloud, and the hours of daylight seem to melt away into cinder gray. That calls for some cozy comforts. And look at this: some new acoustic instrument engineering, and a tiny acoustic piano. This is not a toy piano — which is a lovely instrument, just in fact, I’d argue not a piano at all. Toy pianos, with metal (or sometimes glass or xylphone) bars, are essentially their own class of percussion instrument that happens to have a piano-style keyboard manual. No, this is a wonderfully scaled-down acoustic piano, as in, honey I shrunk the spinet.
articleBody: # The gentle sounds of a tiny acoustic piano from Denmark - CDM Create Digital Music MusicMusic techTech ## The gentle sounds of a tiny acoustic piano from Denmark Peter Kirn - November 25, 2026 Add comment In northern Europe, it’s that time of year that disappears under a thick blanket of cloud, and the hours of daylight seem to melt away into cinder gray. That calls for some cozy comforts. And look at this: some new acoustic instrument engineering, and a tiny acoustic piano. This is not a toy piano — which is a lovely instrument, just in fact, I’d argue not a piano at all. Toy pianos, with metal (or sometimes glass or xylphone) bars, are essentially their own class of percussion instrument that happens to have a piano-style keyboard manual. No, this is a wonderfully scaled-down acoustic piano, as in, honey I shrunk the spinet. (To this day, my favorite instrument of all time was the childhood Everett spinet, a friendly US-built model. Helsinki-based pianist Antti Kujanpää recorded this beautiful demo, which has every right to go a bit viral at this moment on Earth. (He didn’t even do a thumbnail looking surprised pointing at anything! See?) They really did manage to make it small. The Danish-built Keybird L1, supporting by a crowdfunding campaign of all things, is only 39 kg, 70x115x55 cm, but still has four octaves and you can play it with even-softer felt engaged, and it comes with a tuning key. It’s clearly a piano you would have a very different relationship with than the 19th century monster we’ve inherited. It’s a piano you can tune. It’s a piano you can carry around. I’m intrigued by the phrase “one of the smallest acoustic pianos on the market.” It’s the smallest I’ve seen. Optional add-ons give it MIDI capabilities and Helpinstill pickups, plus the usual accoutrements like a tuning kit and road case. Some outlets picked this up earlier this year, but the appearance of this video indicates that they are now starting to ship, as promised, this quarter. Antti’ has this lovely solo album, too. Listen, let me tell you, I like music. Sometimes I like it to sound like a swarm of alien bees set to tear out your eardrums, and sometimes I like it to sound like this. Afterimage by Antti Kujanpää That being said, I do hope there’s some angular, dissonant music composed for it, too! I imagine that could be fragile and strange, like a snowflake on a moon of Jupiter. Uh, if anyone has one and wants a composer, I volunteer. If you want one yourself, it’s €3.750,00 incl. VAT — but expect some time to get one. Over ten years ago, I wrote an extended feature on another new acoustic piano — the Una Corda, now positively enormous at 100 kg. > Acoustic Revelation: Inside the Una Corda, the 100kg, 21st Century Piano Built for Nils Frahm But here as now, even as someone who’s spent long hours at the desk of a Steinway grand, I am absolutely overjoyed to see the tyranny of the Steinway Model D-274 finally seeing some resistance. (Even competing models from Yamaha and others are closely related in design.) We’ll always have the Model D. It’s long past time to have something else, too. articleBody:
I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.

Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.

Coding agents in November 2025

Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model.

In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:

Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.

This held up.

Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025.

Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant.

The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself.

Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.

The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work.

Fable class models in June/July

We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.

In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.

After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st.

For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these:

In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug.

A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm.

Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook.

I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well.

These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model.

3D modeling and game development in September/October

Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for.

I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example.

3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa.

Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game. It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play.

I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play!

Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked. My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay.

Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time.

Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games.

The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster.

It feels like another inflection point to me.

Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too?

I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement.

I'm getting so much done with that model right now!

It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42, 1.0a43, and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37, 0.37.1, 0.37.2, 0.37.3, and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks, represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements.

If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it. That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks.

Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand.

## Carl Stumpf

The name Carl Friedrich Stumpf (1848–1936) is historically associated with one of the most important philosophical trends in the early twentieth century, phenomenology. Stumpf supervised Husserl’s habilitation thesis in Halle in 1887 and the latter’s seminal work on phenomenology, Logical Investigations (1900–1901), is dedicated to him in recognition of his friendship and his philosophical contribution to this book. Stumpf is also known as the founder of the Berlin Institute of Psychology, which gave rise to Gestalt psychology, another important current during the early twentieth century and whose main adherents were among others, his students W. Köhler, K. Koffka, W. Wertheimer and K. Lewin. Founder of the Phonogram Archive in Berlin, now under the protection of the UNESCO, he is also considered one of the forefathers of comparative musicology and a pioneer in ethnomusicology. He held positions in the philosophy departments at the universities of Göttingen, Würzburg, Prague, Munich and Halle, before obtaining a professorship at the University of Berlin, where he was also rector in 1907–1908. His two main sources of inspiration in philosophy are Franz Brentano, of whom he was the first student in Würzburg, and Hermann Lotze, who supervised his 1869 doctoral thesis on Plato and his habilitation thesis on mathematical axioms (1870). The philosophical work he left us is as original and as diversified as his academic and institutional achievements. Besides many treatises in the fields of acoustics and musicology, his important contributions to the development of the “new psychology” and to the philosophy of the mind in general should also be noted. His friend William James said of him in his Principles of Psychology (1890: vol. II 282 [ch. XX]) that he was “the most philosophical and profound of all writers; and I owe him much”. His studies in the field of descriptive psychology and phenomenology (known as the science of phenomena) for example, are of particular interest to current research in the fields of philosophy of mind and cognitive sciences.

## 1. Biographical Sketch

Stumpf’s intellectual biography is rich and complex due to his long university career that lasted for more than 50 years, his academic achievements, and his philosophical work. To complete this biographical sketch, the reader is invited to consult Stumpf’s autobiography (published in 1924) and the Sprungs’ biography, published in German under the title Carl Stumpf – Eine Biografie (H. Sprung with L. Sprung 2006).

- 1848 Carl Friedrich Stumpf was born on April 21, 1848 in Wiesentheid in Franconia, Germany.
- 1859–1863 Attended the Gymnasium in Bamberg, studied music and composed several pieces.
- 1864–1865 Attended the Gymnasium in Aschaffenburg where he studied Plato with Hocheder.
- 1865 Entered the University of Würzburg and during his first year studied aesthetics and law
- 1866 Met Franz Brentano on July 14, 1866 during the disputatio of his habilitation and then decided to study philosophy with Brentano. From 1867 to 1870 he attended Brentano’s lectures on the history of philosophy, metaphysics, Comte and positivism and logic.
- 1867–1868 Because Brentano had not been habilitated to supervise dissertations, it was recommended that Stumpf study with Hermann Lotze in Göttingen. He attended Lotze’s lectures on psychology, history of philosophy since Kant, philosophy of nature, and practical philosophy. He also attended lectures from the physiologist G. Meissner and the physician W. Weber.
- 1868 Graduated on August 13, 1868 with a dissertation on Plato and then returned to Würzburg to study with Brentano.
- 1869–1870 Entered the ecclesiastical seminary in Würzburg and resigned in July 1870 due to the influence of Brentano and Lotze.
- 1870 Returned to Göttingen to prepare his habilitation on mathematical axioms under the supervision of Lotze and successfully defended it in October 1870.
- 1870–1873 Lectured at the University of Göttingen where he founded the Eskimo society along with his friend Felix Klein. He also met G. Fechner and probably G. Frege, who studied in Göttingen during this period.
- 1873 Published an important treatise on the origin of space perception ( Über den psychologischen Ursprung der Raumvorstellung) , and dedicated it to Lotze.
- 1873–1879 Was appointed to his first professorship at the University of Würzburg at the age of 25 to replace Brentano, who moved to Vienna in 1874.
- 1878 Married Hermine Biedermann (1849–1930).
- 1879–1884 Moved to Prague and was joined there by his friend Anton Marty in 1880. He developed professional contacts with Mach and maintained a close relationship with Ewald Hering.
- 1882 Was visited by William James in Prague and this encounter led to the beginning of a lasting friendship between both philosophers.
- 1883 Published the first volume of Tonpsychologie .
- 1884–1889 Replaced H. Ulrici at the University of Halle and became a colleague of Georg Cantor and J. E. Erdmann.
- 1887 Husserl submitted his habilitation thesis on the origin of the concept of number under Stumpf’s supervision.
- 1889–1894 Arrived in Munich in 1889 as the successor to K. Prantl.
- 1890 Published the second volume of Tonpsychologie. He also worked with H. Ebbinghaus, H. von Helmholtz, and G. E. Müller, among others, on the prestigious journal Zeitschrift für Psychologie und Physiologie der Sinnesorgane , of which Stumpf was one of the founding editors.
- 1891 Involved in a controversy with W. Wundt and his students on the use of experiments and on Fechner’s law.
- 1894 Joined the philosophy faculty in Berlin after a long period of hesitation; marked the beginning of a new period in his intellectual life.
- 1896 Presided along with T. Lipps the third International Congress of Psychology in Munich.
- 1898 Joined the Academy of sciences in Berlin. Founded the journal Beiträge zur Akustik und Musikwissenschaft , which contains many treatises written by Stumpf and his students.
- 1900 Founded the Institute of Psychology in Berlin, which gave rise to Gestalt Psychology; started the Phonogramm-Archiv in Berlin on the basis of some phonographic recordings of a Siamese company performing in Berlin; in the same year along with F. Kemsies he started the Berlin Gesellschaft für Kinderpsychologie .
- 1900–1901 Husserl’s groundwork Logical Investigations was published and dedicated to Stumpf.
- 1904 Asked by the Board of Education to investigate the well-known case of “clever Hans” and in 1907 the results of this investigation were published by Stumpf and his assistant O. Pfungst in the book Clever Hans (The Horse of Mr. von Osten): A Contribution to Experimental Animal and Human Psychology .
- 1906–1907 Published three important treatises, which were extensively discussed by philosophers and psychologists: “Erscheinungen und psychische Funktionen” (1906b), “Zur Einteilung der Wissenschaften” (1906a) and “Über Gefühlsempfindungen” (1906c).
- 1907–1909 Accepted the honorific position of rector of the University of Berlin; pronounced his first address “Die Wiedergeburt der Philosophie” [“Renaissance of Philosophy”] (1907) on the state of philosophy in Germany since Lotze.
- 1908 Robert Musil, the author of The Man without Qualities , wrote a dissertation on Mach under the supervision of Stumpf.
