articleBody:
Hi folks,

As you might have noticed my blog has undergone a metamorphosis and is now Windows 8 Metro style inspired. It’s also no longer in Silverlight.

What are the top 2 features of this blog?

One of the top two features I’m quite excited about is a home page with flipping tiles. If you haven’t seen it yet head on over to https://justinangel.net/ and have a look.

Another feature I’m quite enamored with are the interactive sidebar charms:

What’s the complete featurelist?

Posting from Windows Live Writer

Tiles Home Page

Flipping animation

TwitPic Tiles

Twitter tile

Article Tile with Topsy Counter

Category Tiles

Sliding Charms Sidebar

Sliding animation

Social Networks Sharing

Interactive Search

Inline Feeds

Contact details

Metro Inspired UI pages

Home Page

Category List

Articles

Hierarchal article comments

Back office Management

RSS 2.0 and Atom 1.0 Feeds

User Friendly URLs

SEO: Site Map and Robots.txt

Google Analytics

Full Source code

What technologies were used?

ASP.Net MVC3 Razor View Engine: User interface front end.

ASP.Net Dynamic Data: The back office management portal.

HeadJS: Used to load Javascript files in parallel and add HTML5 cross-browser support with some poly-fills.

jQuery: Javascript minimum bar.

jQuery.Templates: Used to render hierarchical comments at the client side.

jQuery.Validate: Used to validate comments at the client side.

jQuery.QuickFlip: Used to create the flipping home page tiles.

jQuery.highlightText: Used to highlight text during searches.

SQL Server 2008:  Database.

Entity Framework: Database OR/M.

MSTest: Unit testing framework.

RhinoMocks: Unit Test mocking.

Unity: Inversion of control framework.

WCF Syndication Services: RSS 2.0 and Atom 1.0 feeds.

Starbucks: Supplier of caffeine.

What happened to your Silverlight blog?

I consider my online presence to be a playground I can use to experiment with. It’s all about trying new things and figuring out what works and what doesn’t. I consider my Silverlight blog to be a huge success, it worked for 2 years and with the exception of some minor justifiable UX complaints I really liked it.

You shouldn’t read anything into my personal technology choices. I rewrote this blog because I felt like it.

Feel free download the Silverlight Weblog @ http://silverlightweblog.codeplex.com/

Is MetroBlog open source?

Yes it is. The source code is open source under MS-PL and can be downloaded from codeplex @ http://MetroBlog.codeplex.com

Tell me more about your home page tiles…

The home page actually displays data from multiple data sources (Blog posts, Twitter, TwitPic and Topsy). And by using flipping tiles I’m able to convey more data in the same screen real-estate.

Over here you can see where the latest blog posts come from:

And the Twitter counter comes from http://topsy.com.

Next we’ve got the Category tiles for the home page:

Another data source is TwitPic showing the latest TwitPics on my account:

And finally there’s a tile with my latest tweet:

The combination of that rich data in a cohesive UX is something that I’m quite happy about.

Thank You!

I’d like to thank the beta testers who helped make this blog significantly better.

Chris Walsh (@ChrisWalshie)

Martin Rauscher (@Hades32)

Anoop Madhusudanan (@amazedsaint)

Aleksandr Sasha K. (@Arktronic)

Rodrigue Hajjar (@rodrigue_)

Matt Hidinger (@matthidinger)

@choudeshell

I’d also like to thank every single open source developer who contributed to the frameworks I’m using.

Comments? Thoughts? Feedback? Something sucks?

Sound off in the comments! Please, I really could use your feedback.

Sincerely,

-- Justin Angel

articleBody:
Every month, we share opportunities for artists and designers, including open calls, grants, fellowships, and residencies. Make sure you never miss out by joining our monthly [Opportunities Newsletter](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/newsletter/opportunities/).

**[Fall $1,800 Innovate Grants for Art + Photo](https://innovateartistgrants.org)** **Featured**
Innovate Grant awards two $1,800 grants each quarter to one visual artist and one photographer. Nine honorable mentions in each category are also featured on the Innovate Grant platform and join a growing creative community of esteemed artists. Applicants must be 18 years and older, and all media and genres are accepted. All applicants retain the right to the work they submit.
**Deadline: 11:59 p.m. PST on December 15, 2026.**

**[Bryson County Retreat](https://www.brysoncountyretreat.org/)** **Featured**
Practicing artists of any background and at any stage of their career are encouraged to apply for a 2027 residency at Bryson County Retreat. Residency periods can be flexible, but month-long stays are suggested. Bryson County is designed to provide ample living and working space and inspirational settings where an artist may work free from the distractions and responsibilities of day-to-day life. The program includes free lodging near tannic dark water lakes, sprawling live oaks, and drooping Spanish moss at the headwaters of the Santa Fe River in north central Florida.
**Deadline: Rolling.**

**Open Calls**

**[Wildlife Photographer of the Year](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/wildlife-photographer-of-the-year/competition.html)** *(International)*
Alongside its conservation message, this prestigious global competition is hosted by London’s Natural History Museum to champion the work of photographers, whether professional or amateur, young or older, or using top-of-the-range equipment or smartphones. Photographers are eligible for myriad awards, with a Grand Title prize of £15,000. The entry fee is £35 (free for Young WPY contest).
**Deadline: 11:30 p.m. GMT on December 3, 2026.**

**[Responsa Foundation Open Call for Textile Art](https://responsafoundation.com/2026/10/13/this-memory-competition/)** *(International)*
The Responsa Foundation champions projects that create meaningful social impact and foster public engagement. The organization is seeking textile artists to submit work for *This Memory,* a group exhibition taking place from September 22 to October 3, 2027, at Burgh House in Hampstead.
**Deadline: December 4, 2026.**

**[Open Call for Public Art Proposals in Moab](https://www.moabarts.org/public-art-application)** (Utah, National)
Moab Arts is accepting proposals for 2027 public art projects. Proposals are welcome for sculpture, murals, three crosswalks, and sticker designs but may include other ideas for different media or locations around the city. Preference is given to local and regional artists.
**Deadline: 11:59 p.m. MST on December 6, 2026.**

**[Material Works Art Award 2026](https://pci.jotform.com/form/262185636090156)** *(International)*
Material Works supports artists through one-time $2,500 awards in exchange for original pieces added to its growing contemporary art collection. The award recognizes artistic excellence and aims to promote career advancement through increasing visibility and exposure. There is a €40 application fee.
**Deadline: December 6, 2026, or when the first 300 artworks submitted, whichever comes first.**

**[Call for Mail Art](https://www.hivebookarts.org/exhibitions/call-for-mail-art)** *(International)*
Hive Center for the Book Arts in Evanston, Illinois, welcomes mail art for the exhibition *love|mark*, which runs from January 1 to February 27. All submissions must arrive at at the center by December 15 for inclusion in the show.
**Deadline:** **December 15, 2026.**

**[Sony Future Filmmaker Awards](https://www.sonyfuturefilmmakerawards.com/)** *(International)*
The Sony Future Filmmaker Awards is a major program providing opportunities for creators and filmmakers. The shortlisted filmmakers are flown to Sony Pictures Studios in Culver City, California, to attend an awards ceremony and an industry immersion program. Categories include fiction, nonfiction, animation, immersive, student, and vertical format.
**Deadline: 7 a.m. CST on December 15, 2026.**

**[GLEAM 2027 Request for Proposals](https://www.olbrichgleam.org/submit-a-proposal)** *(International)*
Olbrich Botanical Gardens in Madison, Wisconsin, invites proposals for temporary, large-scale, light-based artwork for *GLEAM*, a public art exhibition. The show will be open to the public from August 28 to October 23, 2027.
**Deadline: 11:59 p.m. CST on January 6, 2027.**

**[Visual Arts Prize IDEA – Vila d’Amer](https://www.ideagc.com/en/idea-mundoarti/)** *(International)*
Apply for this inaugural prize open to artists working in all visual arts media. Two winning artworks, with prizes of €3,500 and €1,500, will become part of the permanent International Visual Arts Collection IDEA – Vila d’Amer.
**Deadline: January 10, 2027.**

**[360 CHICAGO: CloudWalk Call for Artists](https://360chicago.com/cloudwalk-call-for-artists)** *(Chicago)*
One artist will be selected for this major installation in the CloudWalk gallery atop 875 N. Michigan Ave. The selected artist receives a $10,000 commission, and the winning installation will go on view starting April 2027.
**Deadline: January 18, 2027.**

**[World of WearableArt 2027 Competition](https://www.worldofwearableart.com/competition/entry-information)** *(International)*
Entries are now open for the 2027 WOW Competition in Wellington, New Zealand. Awards consist of NZ$200,000 in prizes, including the Supreme WOW Award of NZ$30,000.
**Deadline: February 11, 2027 (international), March 31, 2027 (New Zealand).**

**Grants**

**[The Filmed in Nevada County Grant](https://nevadacityfilmfestival.com/filmedinnc/)** *(International)*
To support filmmakers in the production of work in Nevada County, California, Nevada City Film Festival offers grants between $1,000 and $20,000.
**Deadline: December 1, 2026.**

**[Southern Prize and State Fellowships for Visual Arts](https://www.southarts.org/grants-opportunities/southern-prize-and-state-fellowships-visual-arts)** *(U.S. South)*
The South Arts Southern Prize and State Fellowships acknowledge the highest quality artistic work being created in the American South. The program is open to individual artists living in Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Tennessee. State Fellowships are $5,000, with one awarded per state. These then compete for two Southern Prize tiers of $25,000 and $10,000.
**Deadline: January 15, 2027 (fee waiver request by December 18, 2026).**

**[The Virigina A. Groot Foundation Grants](https://www.virginiaagrootfoundation.org/grants/)** *(International)*
Each year, the Virginia A. Groot Foundation offers three grants to artists who have exceptional talent and a demonstrated ability in ceramic sculpture or sculpture of diverse mediums. The grants are organized into tiers, with the top award providing $60,000, the second award offering $30,000, and the third awarding $20,000.
**Deadline: January 9, 2027.**

**[Foundation for Contemporary Arts](https://www.foundationforcontemporaryarts.org/grants/emergency-grants/)** **[Emergency Grants](https://www.foundationforcontemporaryarts.org/grants/emergency-grants/)** *(U.S.)*
Emergency Grants provide urgent funding for visual and performing artists and poets who have sudden, unanticipated opportunities to present their work to the public, but there is insufficient time to seek other sources of funding or unexpected expenses are incurred for projects close to completion. Each month, the organization makes approximately 15 to 20 grants in the range of $500 to $3,000 each.
**Deadline: Rolling.**

**[National Lottery Project Grants](https://www.artscouncil.org.uk/ProjectGrants/national-lottery-project-grants-guidance-library)** *(U.K.)*
Both individuals and organizations can apply to Arts Council National Lottery Project Grants. These awards are designed to focus on specific projects with starting and ending dates including festivals and carnivals, dance, libraries, literature, museums, music, theater, or visual arts programs. There is no maximum threshold for the fund.
**Deadline: Rolling.**

**[Black Artists Grant](https://commonwealthfoundation.com/opportunity/black-artists-grant/)** *(U.K.)*
The Black Artists Grant offered by Creative Debuts is no-strings-attached financial support to help Black artists. Selected applicants receive £500, and applications are reviewed monthly.
**Deadline: Rolling.**

**[The Adolf and Esther Gottlieb Emergency Grant](https://www.gottliebfoundation.org/emergency-grant)** *(International)*
This program provides one-time financial assistance to qualified painters, printmakers, and sculptors whose needs resulted from an unforeseen catastrophic incident and who lack the resources to meet that situation. Awardees typically receive $5,000 and up to $15,000.
**Deadline: Rolling.**

[Pollock-Krasner Foundation Grant](https://pkf.org/apply/) * (International)*
The foundation welcomes applications from painters, sculptors, and artists working on paper, including printmakers. Grants are intended for one year and range up to $50,000. The artist’s circumstances determine the size of the grant, and professional exhibition history will be considered.
**Deadline: Rolling.**

**Residencies, Fellowships, & More**

**[Kent Cultural Alliance Spring 2027 SERVICE Residency](https://kentculture.org/residency/)** *(U.S.)*
Artists are invited to apply for a six-week residency session in Chestertown, Maryland, devoted to the theme of service. Each selected artist will receive a $7,500 stipend for the six-week session, a travel reimbursement up to $1,000, and studio and gallery expense reimbursement up to $1,500.
**Deadline: 5 p.m. EST on December 1, 2026.**

**[Charles Allis Art Museum Artist in Residence](https://www.charlesallis.org/learn_about/artist_in_residence_/)** *(International)*
Located in Milwaukee’s Lower East Side neighborhood, the Charles Allis Art Museum residency program gives one artist the opportunity to engage with the Allis’ collection of more than 800 historic pieces from the early 20th century. The participant receives an $1,800 honorarium and up to a $400 travel stipend.
**Deadline: December 4, 2026.**

**[2026 McKnight Fellowships for Fiber Artists](https://textilecentermn.org/event/applications-open-for-2026-mcknight-fellowships-for-fiber-artists/)** *(Minnesota)*
Each year, the Textile Center awards two unrestricted $25,000 fellowships to post-emerging Minnesota fiber artists who demonstrate exceptional proficiency, sustained practice, and commitment to the field. Fellowship dates are March 1, 2027, to February 28, 2028.
**Deadline: December 7, 2026.**

**[Open AIR Residencies](https://www.openairmt.org/opportunities)** *(International)*
Open AIR is a Missoula-based nonprofit that brings artists and communities together through place-based residencies and public arts programs across Montana. Sessions currently accepting applications include summer 2027, fall 2027, and spring 2028.
**Deadline: December 7, 2026.**

**[Cove Park Awarded Residencies for 2027-28](https://covepark.org/awarded-residencies-2027-2028/)** *(International)*
Located in beautiful Argyll & Bute, Scotland, Cove Park awards funded residencies, in addition to travel, visa, materials, and access allowances when required. (Self-funded Open Residencies and subsidized winter residencies are open on [a rolling basis](https://covepark.org/current/).)
**Deadline: December 11, 2026.**

**[An Talla Solais Càirdeas/The Kinship Residency](https://www.antallasolais.org/opencall)** *(International)*
BIPOC artists working in any medium are invited to apply to this fully funded residency in Ullapool in the Scottish Highlands. The program runs throughout January, February, and March 2027. The residency covers all work space, housing, mentoring, and exhibition costs in addition to a £750 weekly stipend.
**Deadline: December 14, 2026.**

**[Joshua Tree Highlands Artist Residency 2027-28](https://www.jthar.org/)** *(International)*
Joshua Tree Highlands Artist Residency offers time and space amidst the natural beauty of Joshua Tree National Park. Seven-week residencies include scholarship funds, housing, and studio space designed to accommodate a broad range of artistic activity and open studio events. There is a $45 application fee.
**Deadline: December 15, 2026.**

**[ren AiR](https://www.ren.global/air)** *(International)*
ren is a discovery platform where you share everything that goes into your artistic practice. For its residency, four selected artists will each receive $5,000 to develop and realize a project of their choice, wherever they are based, while sharing their creative journey with the ren community. In addition, eight artists will receive $2,000 prizes.
**Deadline: December 31, 2026.**

**[Ox-Bow Summer Fellowship](https://www.ox-bow.org/fellowship-program)** *(International)*
The Ox-Bow Summer Fellowship offers twelve weeks to slow down and deepen your practice within a creative community. The program will welcome 18 fellows and is open to senior BFA students, MFA students, postgraduates, and artists with comparable professional experience.
**Deadline: January 7, 2027.**

**[Fine Arts Work Center Seven-Month Residency](https://fawc.org/apply/)** *(International)*
The Fine Arts Work Center in Provincetown grants 10 annual fellowships each to visual artists and writers for a seven-month residency that runs from October 1 to April 30. Visual arts fellows are provided with a private furnished apartment and a separate studio, a $1,300 monthly stipend, plus a $1,000 exit stipend to support relocation at the end of the fellowship. There is a $55 application fee until midday on December 1, then $65 until the opportunity closes.
**Deadline: February 6, 2027.**

**[Smithereen Farm Winter Residency](https://www.smithereenfarm.com/winter-residency/)** *(International)*
Smithereen Farm offers affordable, shared, winter housing to farmers and agrarian-adjacent people and creatives. In the winter, its studio spaces and rooms in shared houses are generally rented for $350 per month, which includes access to common rooms, space for studio work or desks, utilities, fast Wi-Fi at Reversing Hall, a carpenter shop, sewing machines, video projection space, and access to the farm’s agricultural library.
**Deadline: Rolling.**

**[Jackrabbit Studios Residency](https://tally.so/r/RGq2yJ)** *(International)*
Jackrabbit Studios is a creative sanctuary and retreat space in the Southern California High Desert that welcomes creatives, healing arts practitioners, and facilitators at any stage of practice to our five acres of secluded and sublime desert expanse to craft a residency tailored to your season of practice. Fees range from $450 per week to $2,000 per week, and pets are welcome for an additional fee.
**Deadline: Rolling.**

body:
# Archaeologists Just Dug Up an Unused, Completely Pristine 6,000-Year-Old Axe Head - Nautilus

## Archaeologists Just Dug Up an Unused, Completely Pristine 6,000-Year-Old Axe Head

A precious object, not a weapon of war

7:00 AM CST on November 26, 2026

Archaeologists have been digging near the Terme di Sorano spa in southern Tuscany since independent archaeologist Stefano Giuntoli noticed a cavity at one of the thermal pools there back in 2024. The subsequent ruins they uncovered have been dated to around 4495–4335 BCE (the Neolithic), and sit on top of an ancient thermal spring. But since the work began, only a few actual objects have been recovered, indicating this was a specialized site, rather than a village or camp where a lot of human activity was happening.

The latest find—a seemingly untouched axe head carved out of greenstone, thought to date back around 6,000 years—further backs up that theory. As the axe head was never used, it’s believed that its presence is symbolic—perhaps used as a part of some kind of religious or spiritual ceremony rather than as a weapon.

Researchers have determined that the axe head is made out of eclogite, a rock formed at great depths and intense pressures. The early European farmers who lived here during the Neolithic may have obtained the carefully crafted piece through trades and exchanges, and ultimately left it as some kind of gift.

If so, it would be considered a votive offering, which is the act of placing objects in a place for sacred reasons, without any intention of getting them back. It’s possible that the thermal spring was seen as a boundary between worlds.

# Archaeologists Just Dug Up an Unused, Completely Pristine 6,000-Year-Old Axe Head - Nautilus

## Archaeologists Just Dug Up an Unused, Completely Pristine 6,000-Year-Old Axe Head

A precious object, not a weapon of war

7:00 AM CST on November 26, 2026

Archaeologists have been digging near the Terme di Sorano spa in southern Tuscany since independent archaeologist Stefano Giuntoli noticed a cavity at one of the thermal pools there back in 2024. The subsequent ruins they uncovered have been dated to around 4495–4335 BCE (the Neolithic), and sit on top of an ancient thermal spring. But since the work began, only a few actual objects have been recovered, indicating this was a specialized site, rather than a village or camp where a lot of human activity was happening.

The latest find—a seemingly untouched axe head carved out of greenstone, thought to date back around 6,000 years—further backs up that theory. As the axe head was never used, it’s believed that its presence is symbolic—perhaps used as a part of some kind of religious or spiritual ceremony rather than as a weapon.

Researchers have determined that the axe head is made out of eclogite, a rock formed at great depths and intense pressures. The early European farmers who lived here during the Neolithic may have obtained the carefully crafted piece through trades and exchanges, and ultimately left it as some kind of gift.

If so, it would be considered a votive offering, which is the act of placing objects in a place for sacred reasons, without any intention of getting them back. It’s possible that the thermal spring was seen as a boundary between worlds.

“The (Terme di Sorano) site is gradually becoming more unique and significant,” Jacopo Francesco Tulipano, one of the team of archaeologists still working at the site, said in a statement (via Google Translate). “The continuation of the work will allow us to gather new data and, once the excavation work is completed, to plan the enhancement of the area.”

articleBody:
Picture Gallery with Views of Modern Rome by Giovanni Paolo Panini, via [WikiArt](https://www.wikiart.org/en/giovanni-paolo-panini/picture-gallery-with-views-of-modern-rome-1758).

Welcome to the reading list, a weekly roundup of news and links related to buildings, infrastructure and industrial technology. This week we look at BAAJA, rayon for missiles, US gas consumption, Cyberarmageddon, and more. Roughly 2/3rds of the reading list is paywalled, so for full access become a paid subscriber.

No essay this week, but I’m working on a long follow up to my [technological search essay](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/technology-as-a-search-problem) that should be out next week.

## Housing and Cities

A neat dataset showing the relationship between excess deaths and temperature in cities around the world. You can really see the sensitivity to high temperatures in places without AC. [[Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/part-one-how-many-people-die-from-extreme-temperatures-and-how-could-this-change-in-the-future)]

The Senate passes the permitting reform bill BAAJA. [[NYT](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/climate/senate-passes-baaja-permitting-bill-energy.html)] And Kalshi now gives BAAJA a 75% chance of becoming law. [[Kalshi](https://kalshi.com/markets/kxpermitbill/american-affordability-and-jobs-act/kxpermitbill-26sep)] And New Mexican Senator Martin Heinrich is in the Economist arguing for BAAJA. “ The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act—which the Senate voted to advance on November 9th and which I co-sponsor with another Democrat and two Republicans—does not remove environmental considerations, the ability to litigate projects or the ability for local communities to comment. Those are necessary. But it does make these reviews a standardised part of a predictable process.” [[The Economist](https://www.economist.com/by-invitation/2026/11/15/a-plan-to-end-americas-most-expensive-bottleneck?giftId=ZDFhYjYzMTYtM2UxZi00Njg0LTk4NzEtMWM4NzNlZDk3OTdl)]

New type of nimbyism just dropped: people opposed to delivery drones flying over their backyard. [[WSJ](https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/amazon-delivery-drones-4807e976?st=wrqyyy)]

How Dubrovnik, the Croatian city where King’s Landing scenes were shot in Game of Thrones, is coping with huge masses of tourists and (checks notes) Montenegrin drug cartels. [[The Times](https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/article/how-to-save-a-city-from-mass-tourism-when-the-mob-wants-you-dead-0g7d626m2)]

## Manufacturing

From the annals of manufacturing bottlenecks: producing more Patriot missiles requires, among other things, a specialized rayon fabric called Raycarb, processed by a single US company who sources it from a tiny number of companies (apparently just two), who are unable or unwilling to ramp up capacity as fast as the US would like. “ Only one rayon product of this kind is approved for use in the most advanced Patriot missiles, and it comes from the Kansas factory of a single supplier, Park Aerospace. With Patriot stockpiles shrinking, the Pentagon official pushed Park for more rayon to help ramp up missile production. It soon became clear that the company’s hands were tied. The problem lay not in Kansas but thousands of miles across the Atlantic near the vineyards of Bordeaux in France. That’s where Park’s supplier, ArianeGroup—a maker of space rockets and ballistic missiles—produces the carbonized rayon fabric, which it then ships to Park for further processing. ArianeGroup had been clear that supply was limited. ” [[WSJ](https://www.wsj.com/world/europe/patriot-missile-rayon-problem-3f39dc98)]

Manufacturing automation startup Hadrian is buying Kutztown Foundry and Machine, a company that makes castings for, among other things, nuclear submarines. [[Manufacturing Dive](https://www.manufacturingdive.com/news/hadrian-acquiring-kutztown-foundry-machine-f6-upgrade-expand-pennsylvania/874947/)]

The US Marine Minerals Administration, formerly the BOEM, held an auction for seabed mining rights on 31 million acres of seabed near American Samoa. [[Maritime Executive](https://maritime-executive.com/article/trump-administration-auctions-deep-sea-mining-areas-at-20-cents-per-acre)]

China produces a lot of air conditioners. [[X](https://x.com/simongerman600/status/2120487160621015178?s=20&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email)]

Apparently Tesla will sell you a Cybercab, under a somewhat strict set of conditions. “ Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.” And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.” [[Electrek](https://electrek.co/2026/11/13/tesla-cybercab-personal-use-orders-299-subscription-geofence/)] And a factory to produce Tesla’s Optimus is under construction at Giga Texas. [[YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SBnEKGe3i14&t=210s)]

A bunch of planned naval vessels have been cut by the US Senate appropriations committee. [[X](https://x.com/LegasovAnalytic/status/2122539419152568761)]

The GAO says the F-35 program has about 26 million spare parts, collectively worth about $31 billion, spread around 700 sites around the world. [[Tom’s Hardware](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/pentagon-struggles-to-account-for-usd31-billion-in-missing-f-35-aircraft-parts-weeks-after-shipment-was-swiped-by-china-tracking-of-estimated-26-million-parts-is-outdated-inaccurate-and-incomplete-says-watchdog)]

Tips for Brainstorming 100 Ideas an Hour

Bing Gordon is the former Chief Creative Officer of Electronic Arts, Amazon board member, and a partner at Kleiner Perkins.

He served on Amazon’s board for more than a decade, a seat he earned after giving Jeff Bezos five ideas. The first was Amazon Prime. Bing describes the week two directors told him they wanted to resign, and the fix he proposed: Bezos opens each meeting with what’s on his mind, and six-page memos replace slide decks.

He explains Bezos’s first rule for the board, “first, do no harm,” and the “institutional no” Bezos wanted the board to help Amazon avoid. He lays out the three behaviors Bezos looks for in people who are right a lot, why Bezos dropped one-on-ones, and how every Amazon candidate faces a seven-person interview loop built on the leadership principles.

Bing then turns to what games taught him. He explains why moving a game from an 80 to a 90 doubles sales, why Steven Spielberg recut films until nobody left their seat, and how expansion packs for The Sims shaped his pitch for Prime.

He shares the David Ogilvy lessons that never made the books, including that 90% of people who recall an ad remember the headline and only 25% remember the body copy.

**Available Now: [YouTube](https://youtu.be/EsNvJrkgAr4?si=9bYvgZBHNosigLKe) | [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/2D0zv8io3fTmXKK92a4cHk?si=3359859315f34cd2)**|**[Apple Podcasts](https://podcasts.apple.com/ca/podcast/learning-from-bezos-jobs-and-spielberg-bing-gordon/id990149481?i=1000803770770) | [X](https://x.com/shaneparrish/status/2125200843481711087?a=P9Pgv1GUv1mvTxjPAGk&s=20) | [Transcript](https://fs.blog/knowledge-project-podcast-transcripts/bing-gordon/)**

## Tiny Lessons

Some of my favorite ideas and lessons from this episode.

**Founders, Leadership, & Boards**

- “The board members who say, ‘You should do this, you should do this,’ are dangerous, especially if they’re confident and handsome.”
- “Adult supervision usually means somebody who’s over the hill, has a great resume and is not willing to roll up their sleeves.”
- “The board’s number one job should be help the founder be a learning machine and see the future.”
- “Behind closed doors, we have a debate. As a manager and team, when we walk out the door, we never second guess each other in public.”
- “Don’t argue with tone of voice, but argue with data, put the problem out in the middle of the room, and then let’s come up with a point of view.”
- Push the ability to say yes as far down in the organization as possible, or layers of bureaucracy will create an institutional no that kills your speed.

**Decision-Making, Learning, and Culture**

- “People who are right a lot are constantly willing to change their mind.”
- “Most humans have trouble updating their decision process with new data.”
- “It’s very likely that the founders who tap out at about 500 people have voted not to keep learning.”
- “The values you espouse have no correlation to company success. What’s correlated is the values you espouse get built into the company daily fabric, and that’s what’s important.”
- “Always know more than anybody in the room about your client’s business.”
- Skeptical optimists win because they can hold a big, life-changing idea in one hand while clearly seeing how it might fail in the other.

**Creativity, Quality, and Product**

- “The good to great usually happens after everybody’s worn out.”
- “The people that you hear about at the top of their game almost all push crazily when other people think they’re done.”
- “The beginning of great creativity is generating a lot of ideas.”
- “Trust your instincts and test your ideas.”
- “Engineers tend to value their work based on how hard it was to do, not how valuable it is to the customer. So you need to give them gaps around customer experience, not around engineering challenge.”
- “Most economists think that the perfect price is a single point and it turns out the perfect price is always a range and you can influence that through emotion.”
- If you have to tell customers you are high quality, they assume you are cheap.

**Investing, Motivation, and Life**

- “Pay attention to your stupid ideas. If people tell you it’s stupid, what they’re really saying, it’s one end of the bell curve or the other, and now your job is to figure out which.”
- “The stuff that everybody likes is usually not a great investment. Could be an okay investment, not a great investment.”
- Stop spending your energy trying to fix your losers and put it into riding your winners.
- If you want people to stay engaged in a game where they don’t always win, create a second currency that rewards their participation. (Think Casinos).

title: The Hidden Spiegeltent in Chicago, Illinois
subtitle: These round wooden dance halls, lined with mirrors and stained glass, went from fair to fair.

articleBody:
Spiegeltents were made to travel. These round wooden dance halls, lined with mirrors and stained glass, went from fair to fair. They went up fast and came down fast. The one on Randolph Street is not going anywhere. It was built indoors, on the 14th floor of a Loop building.

The building opened in 1926. Rapp & Rapp designed it, with the Oriental Theatre movie palace on the lower floors. The theater is now the James M. Nederlander Theatre. The whole building stands on the site of the Iroquois Theatre, where a fire in 1903 became one of the deadliest in American history.

High above the theater, the architects put a large hall for Masonic meetings. It sat empty for decades. Later it was turned into offices, and a dropped ceiling hid the room completely. When the building was converted into the Cambria Hotel, workers took that ceiling down and found the old hall again, steel bow trusses and all.

In 2019 the tent came over from Belgium in pieces, about 4,000 of them. Belgian tent builders put it together inside the hall, the traditional way, with no nails. It is about 72 feet across. From the hall, it looks like a small circus parked under factory trusses. Inside, there is carved wood, stained glass, velvet and mirrors everywhere. The mirrors are not just for looks. They let guests see around the posts that hold up the roof.

Since October 2026, the tent has been the home of Kermess by Circensia, which kept it right at the center of the room.

body:
# Dresden - BSW-Co-Vorsitzender De Masi schließt Koalitionen mit AfD aus - Richtungsstreit auf dem Parteitag erwartet

Fabio de Masi, BSW (Jens Kalaene / dpa / Jens Kalaene)Zwar gebe es dort einige gemeinsam beschlossene Anträge, doch handele es sich um eine nur geringe Zahl, so de Masi weiter. Er warf Linken und Grünen vor, in dem Bundesland nicht auf Angebote der Zusammenarbeit mit seiner Partei eingegangen zu sein.

### Auch Ko-Vorsitzende Mohamed Ali gegen Koalitionen

Auch die Ko-Vorsitzende Mohamed Ali lehnte Koalitionen mit der AfD ab. Es gebe große Unterschiede zwischen beiden Parteien, sagte sie im ZDF. Wenn aber ein Antrag gut sei, dann werde man ihm zustimmen - egal von wem er komme.Der bisherige Leitantrag der BSW für den Parteitag untersagt Koalitionen oder Tolerierungen einer AfD-Regierung, ermöglicht aber schriftliche Vereinbarungen über inhaltliche Zusammenarbeit mit der unter anderem in Sachsen-Anhalt als gesichert rechtsextrem eingestuften Partei.

### Innerparteiliche Diskussion über Haltung zur AfD

Die Spitzenkandidaten des BSW in Sachsen-Anhalt, Schulze und Wittig, wollen eine sachbezogene Zusammenarbeit mit der AfD. Für diesen sogenannten "Magdeburger Weg" sprechen sich auch andere führende BSW-Politiker aus - vor allem aus den ostdeutschen Bundesländern. BSW-Gründerin Sahra Wagenknecht unterstützt eine Annäherung an die AfD ausdrücklich: Der "Magdeburger Weg" biete für die Partei "große Chancen", heißt es in einem Positionspapier der BSW-Grundwertekommission, der Wagenknecht vorsteht. Eine Koalition mit der AfD oder die Tolerierung einer AfD-Minderheitsregierung wird aber abgelehnt.

### "Keine Tolerierung einer AfD-Regierung"

Die Annäherung zur AfD sorgt allerdings parteiintern für Widerstand. Die BSW-Gründungsmitglieder Dagdelen, Ernst, Leye und Rabie schrieben in einem Gastbeitrag für die "Zeit", zum Gründungskonsens des BSW habe "die klare politische Abgrenzung zur AfD" gehört - dieser werde jetzt infrage gestellt. "So richtig es war, die Brandmauer abzulehnen, die ausschließlich der AfD genutzt hat, so falsch ist es, sich mit der AfD gemein zu machen."Der "Magdeburger Weg" drohe "zu einer politischen Kooperation mit der AfD zu werden", ohne je im Bundesvorstand beschlossen worden zu sein, kritisieren die BSW-Politiker. "Dies würde das BSW nachhaltig kompromittieren und auf Dauer politisch überflüssig machen." Sie fordern stattdessen: "Keinerlei Tolerierung einer AfD-Regierung. Keine Kooperationsvereinbarungen. Keine Enthaltung bei alleiniger AfD-Kandidatur für das Amt des Ministerpräsidenten."

### BSW will sich bei Ministerpräsidentenwahl in Sachsen-Anhalt enthalten

In Sachsen-Anhalt findet am 8. Dezember die Wahl des AfD-Politikers Siegmund zum Ministerpräsidenten an. Dafür ist die AfD - zumindest im ersten und zweiten Wahlgang - auf Stimmen aus anderen Parteien angewiesen. Das BSW kündigte an, sich enthalten zu wollen. Ob die fünf Abgeordneten sich daran halten, wird aber schwer nachzuprüfen sein, denn die Wahl ist geheim.Diese Nachricht wurde am 27.11.2026 im Programm Deutschlandfunk gesendet.

Wenn aber ein Antrag gut sei, dann werde man ihm zustimmen - egal von wem er komme.Der bisherige Leitantrag der BSW für den Parteitag untersagt Koalitionen oder Tolerierungen einer AfD-Regierung, ermöglicht aber schriftliche Vereinbarungen über inhaltliche Zusammenarbeit mit der unter anderem in Sachsen-Anhalt als gesichert rechtsextrem eingestuften Partei.

### Innerparteiliche Diskussion über Haltung zur AfD

Die Spitzenkandidaten des BSW in Sachsen-Anhalt, Schulze und Wittig, wollen eine sachbezogene Zusammenarbeit mit der AfD. Für diesen sogenannten "Magdeburger Weg" sprechen sich auch andere führende BSW-Politiker aus - vor allem aus den ostdeutschen Bundesländern. BSW-Gründerin Sahra Wagenknecht unterstützt eine Annäherung an die AfD ausdrücklich: Der "Magdeburger Weg" biete für die Partei "große Chancen", heißt es in einem Positionspapier der BSW-Grundwertekommission, der Wagenknecht vorsteht. Eine Koalition mit der AfD oder die Tolerierung einer AfD-Minderheitsregierung wird aber abgelehnt.

### "Keine Tolerierung einer AfD-Regierung"

Die Annäherung zur AfD sorgt allerdings parteiintern für Widerstand. Die BSW-Gründungsmitglieder Dagdelen, Ernst, Leye und Rabie schrieben in einem Gastbeitrag für die "Zeit", zum Gründungskonsens des BSW habe "die klare politische Abgrenzung zur AfD" gehört - dieser werde jetzt infrage gestellt. "So richtig es war, die Brandmauer abzulehnen, die ausschließlich der AfD genutzt hat, so falsch ist es, sich mit der AfD gemein zu machen."Der "Magdeburger Weg" drohe "zu einer politischen Kooperation mit der AfD zu werden", ohne je im Bundesvorstand beschlossen worden zu sein, kritisieren die BSW-Politiker. "Dies würde das BSW nachhaltig kompromittieren und auf Dauer politisch überflüssig machen." Sie fordern stattdessen: "Keinerlei Tolerierung einer AfD-Regierung. Keine Kooperationsvereinbarungen. Keine Enthaltung bei alleiniger AfD-Kandidatur für das Amt des Ministerpräsidenten."

### BSW will sich bei Ministerpräsidentenwahl in Sachsen-Anhalt enthalten

In Sachsen-Anhalt findet am 8. Dezember die Wahl des AfD-Politikers Siegmund zum Ministerpräsidenten an. Dafür ist die AfD - zumindest im ersten und zweiten Wahlgang - auf Stimmen aus anderen Parteien angewiesen. Das BSW kündigte an, sich enthalten zu wollen. Ob die fünf Abgeordneten sich daran halten, wird aber schwer nachzuprüfen sein, denn die Wahl ist geheim.Diese Nachricht wurde am 27.11.2026 im Programm Deutschlandfunk gesendet.

articleBody:
Imagine you’re in a seat in the theatre. The stage has a back and sides, but is open to the audience. And yet, the actors behave as though they can’t see the rows of people watching. It’s as if there’s a fourth wall.

The fourth wall is the imaginary barrier between the fictional world and the audience in TV, film, or theatre.

As the audience, you are in a privileged position of watching these private scenes play out in front of you.

Origin of the Fourth Wall

An early description of this invisible barrier as a wall comes from our pal Denis Diderot (also of The Diderot Effect) in his 1758 writing Discours de la poésie dramatique (translated):

"Whether you are writing or acting, give no more thought to the spectator than if he did not exist. Imagine a great wall at the edge of the stage separating you from the audience; act as though the curtain had never risen."

I love Denis’ comment about acting as though the curtain had never risen. I’m not an actor, but I would guess that being able to ignore that there’s an audience, or a camera, might help create a more realistic performance.

Breaking the Fourth Wall

Now, you might take issue with Diderot’s notion, especially if you’ve ever been to a pantomime. Many shows don’t treat the fourth wall as a wall. A pantomime is expected to engage the audience by acknowledging that there will be things the audience can see on stage that a character perhaps can’t—“It’s behind you!” Other times the audience are explicitly part of the show.

Some shows have characters turn and share private thoughts directly into the camera, or simply give a knowing glance. This is known as breaking the 4th wall. Phoebe Waller-Bridge did this all the time in Fleabag, making the viewers her confidants in the scene.

We recently enjoyed a family viewing of Monty Python and the Holy Grail, which does it rather spectacularly, merging the medieval and the modern.

Related Ideas to The Fourth Wall

Front Stage, Back Stage

Diagonal Billing

The Third Teacher

Information Radiator

The Diderot Effect

Mean-World Syndrome

Here’s Diderot’s passage in the original French:

"Soit donc que vous composiez, soit que vous jouiez, ne pensez non plus au spectateur que s’il n’existait pas. Imaginez sur le bord du théâtre un grand mur qui vous sépare du parterre ; jouez comme si la toile ne se levait pas."

title: How to Touch the Nothingness Behind Everything: Kahlil Gibran on the Seven Selves
subtitle: A self is an illusion, and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.

articleBody:
A self [is a forest](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/11/09/pando/). A self [is a ship](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/03/08/plutarch-the-ship-of-theseus-ted-ed/). A self [is an illusion](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/10/21/iris-murdoch-unselfing/), and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.

Above all, a self is [a sum of selves](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/04/10/parts/), contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of life.

[Kahlil Gibran](https://themarginalian.org/tag/kahlil-gibran) (January 6, 1883–April 10, 1931), who thought deeply about [the art of becoming yourself over the sweep of life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/04/04/youth-and-age-kahlil-gibran/), takes up this question in one of his signature parable-poems found in his 1918 classic [The Madman](http://www.amazon.com/Madman-His-Parables-Poems/dp/0486419118/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](http://www.worldcat.org/title/madman-his-parables-and-poems/oclc/242642&referer=brief_results) | [free ebook](http://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5616)).

The poem unfolds as a taxonomy of the core animating passions we live with and suffer by — sorrow, ecstasy, infatuation, hate, longing, creative possession — each a trap, a cage, a dooming fate the sufferer yearns to rebel against. Then comes the seventh self, seemingly the most pitiable, for it is the self that appears to live in pointlessness, perpetually facing the void, but in the end the freest: Only the empty self that lusts for nothing can touch the essence of everything. (Gibran would have appreciated [the Japanese concept of ma](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/09/07/ma/).)

Kahlil Gibran

> THE SEVEN SELVES
> by Kahlil Gibran
> In the stillest hour of the night, as I lay half asleep, my seven
> selves sat together and thus conversed in whisper:
> First Self: Here, in this madman, I have dwelt all these years,
> with naught to do but renew his pain by day and recreate his sorrow
> by night. I can bear my fate no longer, and now I rebel.
> Second Self: Yours is a better lot than mine, brother, for it is
> given to me to be this madman’s joyous self. I laugh his laughter
> and sing his happy hours, and with thrice winged feet I dance
> his brighter thoughts. It is I that would rebel against my weary
> existence.
> Third Self: And what of me, the love-ridden self, the flaming brand
> of wild passion and fantastic desires? It is I the love-sick self
> who would rebel against this madman.
> Fourth Self: I, amongst you all, am the most miserable, for naught
> was given me but odious hatred and destructive loathing. It is
> I, the tempest-like self, the one born in the black caves of Hell,
> who would protest against serving this madman.
> Fifth Self: Nay, it is I, the thinking self, the fanciful self,
> the self of hunger and thirst, the one doomed to wander without
> rest in search of unknown things and things not yet created; it is
> I, not you, who would rebel.
> Sixth Self: And I, the working self, the pitiful labourer, who,
> with patient hands, and longing eyes, fashion the days into images
> and give the formless elements new and eternal forms — it is I, the
> solitary one, who would rebel against this restless madman.
> Seventh Self: How strange that you all would rebel against this
> man, because each and every one of you has a preordained fate to
> fulfill. Ah! could I but be like one of you, a self with a determined
> lot! But I have none, I am the do-nothing self, the one who sits
> in the dumb, empty nowhere and nowhen, while you are busy re-creating
> life. Is it you or I, neighbours, who should rebel?
> When the seventh self thus spake the other six selves looked with
> pity upon him but said nothing more; and as the night grew deeper
> one after the other went to sleep enfolded with a new and happy
> submission.
> But the seventh self remained watching and gazing at nothingness,
> which is behind all things.

Couple with Gibran on [silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/11/21/kahlil-gibran-prophet-talking/), then revisit Hermann Hesse on [discovering the soul beneath the self](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/02/18/hesse-soul/).

### donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing *The Marginalian* (which [bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/22/brain-pickings-becoming-the-marginalian/) for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a [donation](https://www.themarginalian.org/donate/). Your support makes all the difference.

### newsletter

*The Marginalian* has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s [what to expect](https://mailchi.mp/brainpickings/janna-levin-rebecca-elson-anne-lamott-james-gleick). Like? [Sign up.](https://www.themarginalian.org/newsletter/)

title: Six Factors That Support Mental Health for Black Youth

articleBody:
On a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an important public health concern. They were having fun even as they took on a heavy task: helping researchers design programs to reduce the skyrocketing suicide rate among Black youth.

In the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades. For those between 10 and 17 years of age, the suicide rate [rose 144% from 2007 to 2020](https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2023-08/2023-august-still-ringing-alarm.pdf). What’s more, Black boys die by suicide more than twice as frequently as Black girls, although the suicide rate for Black girls [increased by 182% between 2001 and 2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10900-019-00678-x).

As the teenagers brainstormed, [Jasmin Brooks Stephens](https://psychology.berkeley.edu/people/jasmin-brooks-stephens), a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby. The moment was a highlight in research she was conducting with the Homeless Children’s Network on improving mental health outcomes for Black youth. Brooks Stephens believed that teens themselves have meaningful ideas to share, and she had worked for eight weeks with these particular teenagers, who were part of the network’s [Jabali Youth Advocacy](https://www.hcnkids.org/jabali-youth-advocacy) organization, culminating in their trip to campus.

“One of the most exciting things was seeing them all jump up and say, ‘Wait, we can make a program for making us feel better? We have the power to do that?’” Brooks Stephens recalled. “Seeing them find and discover that sense of agency in themselves—that was invaluable to me.” It also was one of the few times any of the teens had visited a college campus, she said, an added bonus. In future work, Brooks Stephens plans to translate the results of her study for clinicians and policymakers who are trying to improve suicide prevention for Black youth.

The ongoing project is just one example of how Brooks Stephens is working to address rising suicide rates among Black youth by engaging them in participatory research—an unusual and hopeful approach in suicide prevention studies. “This summer I had the incredible opportunity to work alongside young people to design a program that would help other young people want to live,” she said. “Rather than waiting until a young person is already in crisis, I’m interested in understanding what helps youth thrive—what gives them hope and a sense of possibility and helps them recognize the brilliance they have inside them.”

## A pathway to hope in the face of racism

Despite the growing crisis among Black youth, [suicide rates are dropping for adolescents in the U.S. overall](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt57150/2025-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf). Brooks Stephens finds these statistics revealing: “To me, that suggests that the approaches we have relied on have not adequately addressed the conditions driving suicide risk in Black communities,” she said.

It’s easy to talk about [structural racism](https://news.berkeley.edu/2025/08/14/watch-berkeley-scholar-explain-structural-racism/) as an abstract concept, or personal encounters with racists as disturbing but bounded moments. But grappling with racism heavily impacts Black youth and increases their suicide risk, according to a 2023 report from the [Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health](https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2023-08/2023-august-still-ringing-alarm.pdf). Indeed, Brooks Stephens has published work documenting how racial discrimination and the COVID-19 pandemic, which disproportionately harmed Black Americans, together [worsened suicide risk for Black young adults](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2025-01327-001).

Brooks Stephens’s work is informed by both her research and her own experience of how race can shape young people’s sense of self. “I became aware very early on that Black children are often navigating expectations about who they are supposed to be before they have even had the opportunity to figure out who they are for themselves,” she said. “That has stayed with me—the importance of creating space for Black young people to define themselves, recognize their strengths, and imagine who they want to become.” At the same time, she saw how the stigma surrounding mental health could make it harder for Black youth and families to seek support, even as racism and other chronic stressors were impacting their well-being.

When she took an African American psychology class as an undergraduate at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, with Enrique Neblett, a renowned scholar of race and health who became her mentor, Brooks Stephens saw the connection between those experiences—and found her passion. “I realized that there was an entire field devoted to understanding how racism affects mental health and how Black children come to understand themselves and their racial identity,” she said.

Later, during her doctoral research at the University of Houston, Brooks Stephens worked with Rheeda Walker, an expert on suicide science and African American adult mental health research. Brooks Stephens noticed that there was very limited discussion about building upstream resilience in suicide prevention research—an approach that focuses on child well-being and happiness before the development of a mental health crisis.

“We’re studying why people choose to end their life without understanding what makes people want to live,” she said. For Brooks Stephens, that realization opened up a different way of thinking about suicide prevention, one that made room for the strengths that were often absent from traditional models, such as racial identity, spirituality, family connection, belonging, or hope.

## Focusing on strengths to prevent suicide

Brooks Stephens knows she can’t single-handedly eliminate the racial traumas faced by young Black people. Nor can she end other factors that lead to higher suicide rates in her community, such as systemic injustice or poverty. Instead, she’s focusing on where she can make a difference through her research.

“While I may not be able to eradicate racism, I can help build programs that change how Black young people see themselves and their futures—programs that help them feel grounded in their identity and able to imagine a life that feels worth living,” she said.

*Brooks Stephens and her colleagues identified six positive factors that reduce suicidality among Black youth (courtesy of Jasmin Brooks Stephens).*

As a first step, this year she and her colleagues created the [Black Youth Thriving Framework for Suicide Prevention](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2027-42684-001). It’s based on a literature review that identified six protective factors that can reduce suicidality among Black youth, including family support, community ties, and self-acceptance. “What we’re working to identify now are the strategies that can help cultivate those strengths in young people’s lives,” Brooks Stephens said.

Already, in a [study from 2023](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/00957984211037440), she and her colleagues showed that Black young adults with stronger feelings of self-acceptance are less vulnerable to depression and suicide. Likewise, she has identified [mindfulness and meditation as potential tools](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12671-023-02180-x) for Black Americans in their early 20s to buffer the impulsivity that is often associated with suicide risk.

This approach is a radical departure from the status quo. Right now, resources for preventing suicide orbit around moments of crisis, Brooks Stephens said. When a child shows signs of depression or arrives at a hospital following a suicide attempt, that’s when an intervention is often provided. Brooks Stephens wants to develop research-backed ways to prevent a child from ever getting to that troubling point in the first place.

And, increasingly, she is asking Black young people themselves to help determine what those approaches should look like. Brooks Stephens said that the four teens with whom she worked this summer were not simply research participants; they were collaborators in imagining what suicide prevention could become.

“It’s very uplifting for me because I’m bringing underserved voices into our research and I’m designing solutions,” she said. “And those solutions are how we make kids want to live and love themselves. That’s it. It’s loving themselves, loving their life. That’s what I’m helping them discover.”

title: Most Teens Care, So Why Don’t They Always Help?
subtitle: A student notices a classmate eating lunch alone.

articleBody:
A student notices a classmate eating lunch alone. Another sees a peer being excluded from a group chat. Someone knows a friend has been struggling but hesitates before reaching out. Why?

Most adults assume the challenge is getting young people to care. But after spending years studying adolescent compassion, I have come to believe that caring may not be the central problem.

Many adolescents care deeply.

The question is what happens next.

We often imagine compassion as a straightforward process: Notice suffering, feel concern, take action. Yet anyone who has worked with adolescents knows that the path is rarely so simple. Young people are navigating friendships, social hierarchies, identity development, and concerns about belonging, all while learning how to manage their own emotions. In these moments, compassion is not simply a feeling. It is a decision unfolding within a complex social world.

In our [recent research developing the Youth Compassion Measure](https://doi.org/10.1177/01650254261485170), an assessment of compassionate responding, we find that most adolescents recognize when a peer is struggling. What varies is whether that recognition translates into helping. Across hundreds of students, four factors consistently shape whether compassion becomes action: peer dynamics, social risk, emotional regulation, and intrinsic motivation.

Understanding these factors may help parents, educators, and youth-serving professionals better support compassionate action in young people.

## 1. Compassion has to survive peer dynamics

One of the clearest findings from our work is that adolescents were more likely to help when the person experiencing distress was someone they knew well.

At first glance, this may seem obvious. Most of us are more likely to check on a close friend than a stranger. Yet this finding points to a deeper truth about adolescence: Compassion unfolds within relationships.

During adolescence, friendships become central to daily life. Young people are figuring out who they are, where they belong, and how they fit into their social worlds. Relationships provide security, identity, and connection. Unsurprisingly, those same relationships shape compassionate responding.

This means that compassion is not simply an individual trait. It is also social.

When educators talk about creating compassionate schools, they often focus on [teaching empathy or kindness](https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/how_educators_are_using_kindness_to_transform_schools). Those efforts matter. But our findings suggest that fostering strong, supportive relationships may be just as important. Young people appear more willing to take compassionate action when they feel connected to the people around them.

In other words, belonging may do more than improve well-being. It may help create the conditions that allow compassion to flourish.

## 2. Compassion involves social risk

If relationships explain who adolescents help, social risk helps explain why they sometimes do not.

Consider a common scenario. A student witnesses a peer being teased. They know the behavior is hurtful. They may even want to intervene. Yet stepping forward could carry consequences. They may worry about being judged, excluded, or embarrassed, or becoming a target themselves.

Our findings suggest that adolescents are often weighing these possibilities, consciously or unconsciously, before deciding how to respond.

This is one reason public conversations about bullying can be so frustrating. When videos circulate online, attention quickly turns to the bystanders. Why didn’t anyone help?

The question assumes that recognizing suffering naturally leads to action. But social reality is more complicated.

Young people are often assessing multiple things at once: the seriousness of the situation, who is involved, who is watching, what might happen if they intervene, and what might happen if they do not. What appears from the outside as indifference may actually be a moment of conflict between compassion and self-protection.

This perspective does not excuse harmful behavior or passivity. But it does encourage us to understand helping as a social act rather than a purely moral one.

If we want young people to act compassionately, we need environments where compassionate action is socially supported instead of socially costly.

## 3. Compassion requires emotional regulation

Perhaps the most surprising finding from our study is that recognizing suffering alone did not consistently predict helping.

Many students understood that someone was struggling. The difference was what happened after that recognition occurred.

One of the strongest predictors of compassionate action is distress tolerance, the ability to remain engaged in the presence of emotional discomfort. This matters because witnessing another person’s suffering is often uncomfortable. We may feel sadness, anxiety, uncertainty, helplessness, or fear of saying the wrong thing. Adolescents experience these emotions, too.

Imagine a teenager whose friend is crying. The challenge is not simply recognizing that the friend is upset; it’s navigating the delicate space between overidentifying with another person’s suffering and distancing oneself from it. Too much emotional absorption can lead to overwhelm and withdrawal. Too much distance can lead to disengagement. Compassion requires something different: remaining connected to another person’s experience while maintaining enough emotional balance to respond effectively.

People sometimes assume that compassion and empathy are the same thing. They are not. [Empathy](https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/topic/empathy/definition#what-is-empathy) allows us to resonate with another person’s experience. [Compassion](https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/topic/compassion/definition#what-is-compassion) involves channeling that awareness into a desire to alleviate suffering. Doing so requires emotional regulation. Without it, concern can become overwhelm, uncertainty, or avoidance. Instead of moving toward suffering, we move away from it.

Our findings suggest that compassionate action depends not only on recognizing another person’s distress, but also on the ability to stay present with that distress without becoming consumed by it. In this sense, emotional regulation is not separate from compassion; it helps make compassion possible.

For parents and educators, this finding has important practical implications. Teaching young people how to navigate difficult emotions may strengthen their capacity for compassionate action. Skills such as mindfulness, emotional awareness, reflection, and distress tolerance are not simply tools for managing stress. They may also be the very capacities that help adolescents transform caring into action by staying engaged when helping feels uncertain, vulnerable, or emotionally difficult.

## 4. Compassion needs motivation

Even when adolescents care and have the emotional skills to stay engaged, one additional factor matters: motivation.

In our study, intrinsic prosocial motivation was one of the strongest predictors of helping. Simply put, adolescents who genuinely wanted to help others were more likely to translate concern into action.

This may sound self-evident, but it carries important implications.

Adults often try to encourage helping through external incentives, praise, rewards, or behavioral expectations. While these approaches can influence behavior, our findings suggest that compassionate action is especially powerful when it emerges from internal values and genuine concern for others.

Young people are constantly asking themselves what kind of person they want to be. When helping becomes connected to identity, meaning, and purpose, compassionate action appears more likely to follow.

This suggests that fostering compassion is about more than encouraging kind behavior. It is also about helping young people develop a sense of responsibility toward others and a meaningful connection to shared humanity.

## What gets in the way of compassion?

Taken together, these findings challenge a common assumption.

There is a tendency to treat moments of inaction as moments of moral failure. We see a young person remain silent, fail to intervene, or walk past another person’s suffering, and we assume we understand what happened.

Yet our research suggests that these moments are often more complicated than they appear.

They unfold within social worlds shaped by belonging, friendship, identity, uncertainty, vulnerability, and the deeply human desire to remain connected to others. They are influenced by relationships, social risks, emotional capacities, and personal motivations.

What looks like indifference from a distance may sometimes reflect a struggle between compassion and the realities that make compassionate action difficult.

This perspective shifts the conversation from a question of character to a question of conditions.

Rather than asking whether adolescents are compassionate, we might ask: What conditions help compassion become action?

## Helping caring become action

The encouraging message from this research is that the factors influencing compassionate action are not fixed traits.

Relationships can be strengthened.

School climates can be improved.

Emotional regulation skills can be taught.

Prosocial values can be nurtured.

When we think about compassion this way, the goal becomes larger than helping young people recognize suffering. The goal is helping them develop the capacities that allow caring to become action.

Perhaps this is what adolescence reveals so clearly. The distance between caring and acting is rarely empty space. It is filled with questions about belonging, uncertainty, responsibility, and risk.

Young people are learning to navigate that space every day.

Our responsibility as the adults who support them is not simply to teach them to care. It is to create the relationships, communities, and opportunities that help them act on the care they already possess.

articleBody:
## pliavo’s folding piano compresses seven octaves

Denver-based Pliavo introduces its Fold-and-Go Piano, a portable digital [instrument](https://www.designboom.com/tag/musical-instruments/) whose 84 keys collapse into a compact bundle small enough to carry inside a backpack. Each octave occupies its own rigid section, and a system of hinges allows the otherwise standard [black-and-white](https://www.designboom.com/tag/black-and-white/) keyboard to fold accordion-style into a vertical stack.

At its full length, the seven-octave instrument stretches 113 centimeters (44.5 inches) across a tabletop. Once folded, it measures just 16 centimeters (6.3 inches) along its length and weighs under two pounds. The team has also developed a smaller, five-octave edition with 60 keys.

Pliavo develops a collapsible 84-key digital piano | images courtesy Pliavo via Kickstarter

## a hinged alternative to the roll-up keyboard

Part of the appeal of Pliavo’s [design](https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/pliavo/pliavo-the-84-key-piano-that-goes-with-you) is that it retains the physical geometry of a conventional keyboard. While many compact electronic pianos take the form of flexible silicone mats, here the musician plays across a continuous arrangement of rigid keys with three millimeters of vertical travel.

The mechanics of the folding design come with some compromises. The keys are unweighted and lack velocity sensitivity, which limits the expressive range of the instrument. Pliavo equips the piano with a detachable wireless speaker and a rechargeable battery designed to last around five hours.

a detachable wireless speaker accompanies the portable keyboard

## a portable instrument for music on the move

The piano’s internal sound library comprises 128 instrument tones alongside an equally extensive selection of rhythm patterns. Through Bluetooth or a USB-C connection, the keyboard doubles as a MIDI controller. For a musician traveling with a laptop, an entire seven-octave workspace could occupy a small corner of their luggage.

Pliavo [launched](https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/pliavo/pliavo-the-84-key-piano-that-goes-with-you) the instrument on Kickstarter in November 2026 and has already exceeded its initial funding goal. The team has developed a playable prototype, with refinements to its sound and finishes underway ahead of an anticipated February 2027 delivery.

articleBody:
When Siddhartha Gautama gave his first teaching after enlightenment, it was to five friends in the deer park at Sarnath, not far from Varanasi in the Ganges Valley. Wanting to transmit to them the essence of his breakthrough, he crystallized his insights into what would become known as the four noble truths. These include the truth of the way out of suffering, known as the noble eightfold path: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

The eightfold path offers a way to touch awakening as Gautama did. These insights were not the result of thinking or study, nor were they a creed or philosophical doctrine. They were the fruit of Gautama’s own direct experience and meditative realization, and they conveyed a path that traced a “middle way” between the two extremes of asceticism and indulgence. It was a way, he believed, that could lead anyone to realize understanding, liberation, and peace.

#### “You don’t hurry to get the dishes done quickly so you can get on with something else. You encounter the miracle of life that includes dishes.”

As a species we’re still struggling to find a middle way, to steer a wise course through the extremes of fanaticism, greed, nihilism, rage, and despair. The ancient wisdom of the eightfold path offers eight matrixes that are powerfully relevant today as a guide to help us navigate these extremes and bring a meaningful direction to our daily lives, actions, and relationships.

All elements of the eightfold path inter-are. You cannot extract any of them from the context of the path. So, for example, if you take mindfulness out of the ethical context of the path, it is no longer right mindfulness. All eight elements are interrelated and interdependent. They enhance each other. When practiced deeply, each element of the path contains the other seven within it, and they complement each other to create a complete path to liberation.

My teacher, Thich Nhat Hanh, taught that right mindfulness is at the heart of the eightfold path. So, with the energy of right mindfulness as the foundation, we’re able to develop right concentration. This gives rise to insight or “right view,” which Thich Nhat Hanh described as the “insight of interbeing.” It is this deep view of the world that guides us to an ethical and beneficial life through right thinking, right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right effort. So, when you generate the energy of mindfulness, you are naturally concentrated on the object of your mindfulness, whether it’s your breathing, your body, the sunset, or the presence of the person in front of you.

Photo © Noumae | Dreamstime.com

The energies of mindfulness and concentration naturally give rise to insight, right view. You touch the insight of interbeing between your breath and the earth, or between your body and your ancestors and descendants, or between your heart and the sun in the sky. You realize that you inter-are with the person in front of you.
Already, this insight of interbeing helps us touch peace, joy, and freedom.

Now, with the energy of mindfulness, concentration, and insight, your thinking will naturally be right thinking.

It will be free from discrimination and separation, and on the basis of that thinking, your speech will be right speech and your action right action.

Cultivating right diligence (or effort) in that moment, you’ll be able to see and calm any unwholesome seeds that may get triggered in your consciousness, such as anger or despair, and identify and activate positive seeds, such as gratitude and compassion. With all those energies alive in you, the way you spend your time, energy, and labor—your livelihood—will be “right.” It will be beneficial for you and everyone around you.

Of course, if there’s “right,” there must also be “wrong.” The Buddha’s teaching does assert that there’s a right and wrong way to go about things. There’s a distinction, for example, between “right mindfulness” and “wrong mindfulness,” between “right concentration” and “wrong concentration,” between “right speech” and “wrong speech.” There’s a way of practicing mindfulness, concentration, and the others that goes in the direction of healing and well-being, and there’s a way that goes in the direction of harm and ill-being.

This is where ethics comes into every aspect of the eightfold path. The wrong path *does* exist—it’s the “ignoble” path of wrong view, wrong thinking, wrong speech, and wrong action that leads to suffering for ourselves, for others, and for the planet. It’s the reason why we’re in the state we’re in. And it’s why we need to find another way of being.

You may wonder, how can there be a wrong way to practice mindfulness? Surely *all* mindfulness is beneficial? In 2014, Thich Nhat Hanh’s last year of teaching, he spoke about the importance of not diluting or appropriating mindfulness as it spreads in the West and reaches new audiences and settings. He explained that the first way to distinguish “right” from “wrong” mindfulness is to realize that right mindfulness is not an instrument or tool but *a way*, a path. It cannot be used as a means to an end.

Yet many of us do speak of mindfulness as a tool. We say that with mindfulness we can heal, with mindfulness we can reconcile, with mindfulness we can make more money, and, in applying mindfulness in the military, with mindfulness we can kill the enemy more effectively. To appropriate mindfulness in this way is to instrumentalize it. Used as a means to an end, whether for profit, success, or even for apparently “beneficial” ends, mindfulness loses its true, authentic spirit. In fact, if you extract any of the eight elements out of the wider ethical context of the path, it is no longer “right.”

The image of “path” or “way” is essential to Buddhist spirituality, and yet it may be challenging for those of us educated in Western capitalist countries. We prefer there to be a goal, a destination, a clear program. We may be seeking a powerful, final moment of “grace” or “attainment.” But as Thich Nhat Hanh used to ask us teasingly,
“Why haven’t you ever asked if the Buddha kept practicing after enlightenment?”

The eightfold path is not so much linear as circular, which is why it’s often seen more as an eight-spoked wheel than a list. The Western-educated mind may struggle with this. We want to know where to start and where we end up. We want to know which element is more important.

The eight-spoke dharma wheel symbolizes the eightfold path. Photo: godongphoto / shutterstock.com

But in his later years of teaching, Thich Nhat Hanh revised his translation of the eightfold path to be not merely “the path leading to happiness,” but “the path of happiness.” He taught that in the true spirit of the insight of interbeing, every step along the path leading to happiness *must be happiness itself*. If we suffer along the way, we’ve lost the game already.

This is strong medicine for the Western tendency to sacrifice means for an end, and for the deep energy of running and striving in our culture. And it’s good news. The eightfold path is not a path of thorns or sacrifice. There’s no need to set our jaw or grit our teeth. There’s an art and poetry to the path of spiritual practice. With every step along our journey we can arrive at our destination. With every step, we can touch happiness, peace, and freedom.

It’s true that at any given moment, one aspect of the path may come more to the fore than another. There may be times we spend a few weeks or months developing right concentration and stillness. Or other times when we focus more on transforming habits of speech, or redirecting our livelihood to be more in line with our aspiration. These things take time to nurture and ripen, and cannot happen all at once.

On the other hand, there may be some settings, as simple as washing the dishes, in which we can actively realize all eight elements at once, and touch joy and freedom right in the heart of our daily life. Every aspect of the path can be realized right in the heart of the present moment: you don’t need to practice for ten days or ten years in order to have insight.

Suppose at some point today you need to wash the dishes. While standing at the sink, you generate the energy of mindfulness—mindfulness of your body and breathing, of your feet on the ground and hands in the water. On an out-breath you may release tension in your body, shoulders, and face, and become fully present for yourself, the dishes, and the wonder of life right in this moment.

You don’t hurry to get the dishes done quickly so you can get on with something else. You encounter the miracle of life that includes dishes. Within a few moments, you begin to develop concentration, and looking deeply into the water, the soap, the sponge, and the dish, insight may naturally arise. Can you see the galaxy in the spoon? Can you see the mountains in the plate? Can you see your grandparents’ hands in your own?

With this kind of insight, your thinking will be right thinking. You won’t think, “Why is it always me who has to do the dishes?” As you enjoy every aspect of washing the dishes and cleaning up, our thinking, speech, and action will carry the insight of interbeing, compassion, and nondiscrimination.

With these energies in you, you’ll be able to handle reactions or frustrations as they arise and generate gratitude, peace, and freedom. In that moment, you won’t discriminate between “work” and “life.” Every part of life belongs to the miracle of being alive. And in that moment, you penetrate the matrix of the eightfold path, you realize the Buddha’s insight in your own life, and you touch peace, freedom, joy, and happiness right in the heart of the present moment.
